content.stem: Phased array ultrasonic testing uses a probe made of:
options: Many small elements fired with controlled timing
A single fixed element fired by itself each shot
A row of fixed wedges, each cut to one set angle
One wide crystal split by a slot down the middle
content.explanation: A phased array probe contains many small piezoelectric elements. Firing them with controlled time delays forms, steers, and focuses the beam electronically.
distractors: A single fixed element is a conventional UT probe, not a phased array.
Fixed single-angle wedges are conventional; the array steers electronically.
A slotted single crystal is not a true multi-element array.

content.stem: Phased array sends energy into the part as a:
options: Pulsed ultrasonic wave
A steady continuous wave
A direct current signal
A static pressure push
content.explanation: Like conventional pulse-echo UT, phased array sends short pulsed ultrasonic waves.
distractors: Pulse-echo uses short pulses, not a steady continuous wave.
The elements send ultrasonic pulses, not a direct current signal.
It sends a vibrating sound wave, not a static pressure push.

content.stem: The beam is steered and focused by:
options: Applying small time delays to the firing of each element
Physically tilting the entire probe by hand to every angle
Pumping more couplant in under the moving probe face plate
Heating the elements up so that the beam bends across
content.explanation: Controlled delays between element firings make the individual wavefronts combine into one wavefront at a chosen angle and focal depth, without moving the probe.
distractors: Electronic steering is the point of phased array; physical tilting alone is the conventional approach.
Couplant transmits sound but does not steer the beam.
Heating the elements does not steer the beam.

content.stem: The single steered wavefront forms because the individual element wavefronts:
options: Combine by constructive interference
Cancel out fully and leave no beam
Race past the set material velocity
Shift the firing frequency right up
content.explanation: Timed firing makes the small wavefronts reinforce along the desired direction, producing one effective beam at the chosen angle and focus.
distractors: Complete cancellation would leave no beam.
All wavefronts travel at the material velocity; timing, not velocity, forms the beam.
The firing delays set direction and focus; they do not change frequency.

content.stem: In phased array, the word phased refers to the:
options: Timing (phase) relationship of the element excitations
Color phase shown across the entire display image view
Phases of the moon running across the course of a month
Metallurgical phase change within the base metal grain
content.explanation: Phased describes the controlled timing relationship among the element pulses, which is what forms and directs the beam.
distractors: It does not refer to a display color phase.
It has nothing to do with lunar phases.
It does not refer to a metallurgical phase change.

content.stem: Compared with a single-element probe, a phased array probe can:
options: Produce many beam angles and focal depths from one position
Produce just one single fixed beam angle from each position
Work fully dry with no couplant at all on the part surface
Find only surface flaws lying right at the top part face
content.explanation: By changing the firing delays, the array sweeps angles and focuses at different depths from a single probe position, which a single-element probe cannot do.
distractors: A single fixed angle describes a conventional probe, not phased array.
Phased array still needs couplant to transmit sound into the part.
Phased array is volumetric, not limited to surface flaws.

content.stem: A practical advantage of phased array over single-element scanning is:
options: Faster coverage and electronic beam control
No need to calibrate before the scan starts
No written procedure for the inspection job
No attenuation of sound through the metal
content.explanation: Electronic steering and focusing cover more volume from fewer positions and produce images, speeding inspection. Calibration and procedures still apply.
distractors: Phased array still requires calibration.
A written procedure is still required.
Phased array sound is still attenuated by the material.

content.stem: Phased array can build a cross-sectional image by combining:
options: Many A-scans taken at different angles or positions
One single A-scan taken from a single fixed spot only
A long run of plain thickness readings on a single line
One single wide unfocused pulse fired straight down once
content.explanation: The instrument assembles the many beams into images such as the sectorial (S) scan, giving a cross-sectional view that a single A-scan cannot.
distractors: A single A-scan alone does not form the cross-sectional image.
A line of single thickness readings is not a steered multi-angle image.
One wide unfocused pulse does not build a cross-sectional image.

content.stem: A group of elements fired together to form one beam is called the:
options: Active aperture
Couplant film
The backwall echo
Beam index point
content.explanation: The active aperture is the set of elements used for a given beam. Its size affects beam characteristics such as focusing and near-field length.
distractors: The couplant layer transmits sound; it is not a group of elements.
The backwall is a reflector, not a group of elements.
The index point is the beam exit point, not the element group.

content.stem: Most phased array weld inspection uses the pulse-echo principle, meaning the array:
options: Transmits and receives the sound
Only receives the returning sound
Only transmits the outgoing sound
Uses two separate probes for it
content.explanation: In pulse-echo, the same array transmits the sound and receives the returning echoes, timing them to locate reflectors, as in conventional UT.
distractors: Receiving the echoes is also required to detect reflectors.
Transmitting is also required to insonify the part.
Pulse-echo is one method using the same array for both roles.

content.stem: When a phased array beam passes through a wedge into steel, its refraction follows:
options: Snell's law
The Ohm law
Square law
Faraday law
content.explanation: Refraction at the wedge-to-part interface obeys Snell's law, just as in conventional angle-beam UT, so the refracted angle depends on the velocities.
distractors: Ohm's law concerns electrical circuits, not refraction.
The inverse square law concerns intensity with distance, not refraction angle.
Faraday's law concerns electromagnetic induction, not sound refraction.

content.stem: Electronic focusing of the beam at a depth improves:
options: Resolution and sensitivity at that depth
The material velocity used in the part
The set pulse repetition frequency value
The number of elements set in the array
content.explanation: Focusing concentrates energy at the focal depth, improving the response and resolution of reflectors there compared with an unfocused beam.
distractors: Focusing uses delays; it does not change the material velocity.
Focusing does not set the pulse repetition frequency.
Focusing applies delays to existing elements; it does not change their number.

content.stem: Because angles are produced electronically, phased array can reduce the:
options: Number of separate probes needed for multiple angles
Need to couple the probe down onto the part surface
Sound velocity the part metal carries the beam at
Wall thickness of the part the beam scans through
content.explanation: One array can cover the range of angles that would otherwise require several single-element angle probes, simplifying setups.
distractors: The probe still must be coupled to the part.
Material velocity is a property of the part, not reduced by phased array.
Part thickness is not changed by the inspection method.

content.stem: In phased array angle-beam work on welds, the refracted beam is usually a:
options: Shear wave
Radio wave
Light wave
Quiet wave
content.explanation: As in conventional angle-beam UT, the wedge mode-converts the beam so a shear wave propagates in the part at the refracted angle.
distractors: Radio waves are electromagnetic, not used here.
Light waves are electromagnetic, not the inspection beam.
An inspection beam is ultrasound, not sound-free.

content.stem: Phased array detects a reflector because sound is:
options: Reflected at an acoustic impedance change
Slowed to a stop within the solid base metal
Wholly absorbed by the sound base metal
Turned to light at the far backwall face
content.explanation: A flaw presents an impedance change that reflects sound back to the array, which the instrument times and displays, as in conventional UT.
distractors: A reflector returns sound at an impedance change; sound does not stop in solid metal.
Sound is not completely absorbed by sound material; it returns from the backwall.
Sound is not converted to light in this process.

content.stem: Accurate depth and position readings in phased array still depend on the:
options: Material's sound velocity
The display color palette
The pulse repeat rate set
Number of focal laws used
content.explanation: Depth and beam path are computed from travel time and material velocity, so the correct velocity must be set, just as in conventional UT.
distractors: The palette affects appearance, not the computed depth.
The pulse repetition frequency sets the firing rate, not the depth calculation.
The number of focal laws affects coverage, not the depth-from-velocity calculation.

content.stem: A sectorial (S) scan from one probe position shows reflectors over a:
options: Range of angles swept electronically
One fixed angle set by hand tilting
One fixed-angle A-scan trace only
Plain optical photo of the part face
content.explanation: An S-scan sweeps a range of angles from one position, giving a fan-shaped cross-section, a hallmark capability of phased array.
distractors: A single fixed angle is the conventional approach, not an S-scan.
An S-scan sweeps a range of angles, not one fixed-angle A-scan.
Phased array forms ultrasonic images, not photographs.

content.stem: In phased array, the controlled delays are applied:
options: On both transmit and receive
On the receive side by itself
On the transmit side by itself
On the couplant film itself
content.explanation: Delay laws shape the beam on transmission and are also applied on reception, so the array focuses and steers in both directions.
distractors: Receive delays are also used to focus the returning signals.
Transmit delays are also used to form the outgoing beam.
Delays are applied to elements, not to the couplant.

content.stem: The energy a phased array probe emits into the part is:
options: High-frequency sound
A low audible hum
A steady light beam
A direct heat flow
content.explanation: Phased array emits high-frequency ultrasonic sound, above the audible range.
distractors: The frequency is ultrasonic, well above an audible hum.
It sends mechanical sound waves, not a beam of light.
It sends vibrating sound energy, not a flow of heat.

content.stem: A typical phased array probe contains:
options: Many elements, often 16, 32, or 64
One single fixed element fired by itself
No elements, just one solid face
Thousands of tiny moving pieces
content.explanation: Common arrays use element counts such as 16, 32, or 64, grouped into apertures for each beam. Confirm the specific probe against its data sheet.
distractors: A single element describes a conventional probe.
A phased array probe must have elements to function.
The elements are fixed, not thousands of moving parts.

content.stem: As in conventional UT, a higher probe frequency generally gives:
options: Better resolution but less penetration
Better penetration but less resolution
No change to resolution or penetration
A beam down in the plain audible range
content.explanation: Higher frequency shortens the wavelength, improving resolution but attenuating faster, so penetration drops, the same trade-off as conventional UT.
distractors: Higher frequency improves resolution and reduces penetration, not the reverse.
Frequency does change resolution and penetration.
Ultrasonic frequencies are above the audible range.

content.stem: A key inspection benefit of phased array is the ability to:
options: Record encoded data for later review
Wipe the data clean after each scan
Skip all documentation for the job
Do away with the written procedure
content.explanation: Position-encoded scanning stores the data so images can be reviewed, reported, and archived, supporting traceability.
distractors: Data is retained, not auto-erased.
Documentation is still required.
Recorded data does not replace the written procedure.

content.stem: The near-field length of a phased array aperture depends mainly on the:
options: Aperture size, frequency, and velocity
Couplant under the moving probe face
Scanning speed set along the weld line
Display palette chosen for the screen
content.explanation: As with any transducer, near-field length grows with aperture size and frequency and varies with velocity, affecting where focusing is effective.
distractors: Couplant transmits sound but does not set the near-field length.
Scanning speed affects data sampling, not the near-field length.
The display palette affects appearance, not the near-field length.

content.stem: Steering the beam to very large angles tends to:
options: Reduce sensitivity and beam quality
Raise sensitivity and beam quality
Change the probe's firing frequency
Cool the entire probe down each shot
content.explanation: Element directivity and spacing limit how far the beam can be steered before sensitivity falls and artifacts grow, so steering ranges are kept within limits.
distractors: Sensitivity falls, rather than improving without limit, at extreme angles.
Steering does not change the probe frequency.
Steering does not cool the probe.

content.stem: At Level I, a phased array technician primarily:
options: Sets up and runs scans and records data under direction
Writes the inspection procedure used for the entire site
Approves the accept and reject criteria for each job
Does the final flaw sizing and evaluation on the job
content.explanation: A Level I operates the equipment, calibrates, scans, and records under direction; procedure writing, criteria, sizing, and evaluation are higher-level tasks.
distractors: Writing the procedure is above the Level I.
Approving acceptance criteria is above the Level I.
Final sizing and evaluation are Level II responsibilities.

content.stem: Producing many angles from a fixed aperture is a sectorial scan; stepping a fixed angle along the array is a:
options: Linear (E) scan
A sectorial scan
A compound scan
A single A-scan
content.explanation: An electronic linear (E) scan keeps the angle constant and moves the active aperture along the array, while an S-scan sweeps angles from one aperture.
distractors: A sectorial scan sweeps angles from a fixed aperture, not a stepped fixed angle.
A compound scan mixes motions; stepping one angle along the array is linear.
A single A-scan is one beam, not a stepped linear scan.

content.stem: Unwanted beams that can appear due to element spacing are called:
options: Grating lobes
Backwall echo
Surface waves
Couplant echo
content.explanation: When element pitch is large relative to the wavelength, grating lobes form and can cause spurious indications, so probe design and setup control them.
distractors: A backwall echo is a normal reflection, not a grating lobe.
A surface wave is a wave mode, not a grating lobe.
A couplant echo is not the spacing-related artifact called a grating lobe.

content.stem: The set of time delays that defines one beam is called a:
options: Focal law
Wedge law
Gain rule
Cable law
content.explanation: A focal law is the table of per-element delays (and apodization) that produces a specific angle and focus. The instrument applies a focal law for each beam.
distractors: There is no couplant law in phased array.
Gain is a separate amplitude setting, not the delay set.
There is no cable law defining the beam.

content.stem: Besides the A-scan, phased array commonly displays:
options: S-scan and other image views
Just one number on the screen
Just a single A-scan trace
Only a numeric thickness value
content.explanation: Phased array shows the A-scan plus image views such as the S-scan, helping visualize reflectors. Interpretation of these is a higher-level task.
distractors: Phased array shows more than a single number.
Phased array shows image views, not just a single A-scan trace.
It shows S-scans and images, not only a numeric thickness value.

content.stem: Phased array still requires couplant because sound:
options: Does not travel well across an air gap
Moves far worse through metal than air
Soaks straight into the dry steel face
Is a light wave needing a clear lens
content.explanation: An air gap reflects nearly all the sound, so couplant is used to transmit sound from the wedge or probe into the part, as in conventional UT.
distractors: Sound travels far better through metal than through air.
Sound needs a couplant path; it does not soak into dry steel.
Sound is a mechanical wave, not light.

content.stem: A phased array instrument fires and reads many elements using:
options: Multiple pulser and receiver channels
A single fixed pulser-receiver channel
One shared timing clock for all elements
A hand switch toggled for each element
content.explanation: The instrument has many pulser and receiver channels (or multiplexing) to drive and read the elements with the required timing.
distractors: A single fixed channel could not independently time many elements.
Independent timing per element needs many channels, not one shared clock.
Elements are driven electronically by channels, not a hand switch.

content.stem: Before scanning, the angles, coverage, and probe positions are defined in a:
options: Scan plan
Job report
Kit manual
Cal sheet
content.explanation: A scan plan specifies the focal laws, coverage, and probe placement so the inspection meets the procedure. A Level I follows it.
distractors: The inspection report records results; it does not pre-define coverage and positions.
The equipment manual covers operation, not the joint-specific coverage plan.
A calibration certificate records calibration, not the scan coverage and positions.

content.stem: To cover a weld fully with angle beams, the technician often scans:
options: From both sides of the weld as the plan requires
From one fixed point set out on the plate face
Without moving the probe along the entire weld
Across only the weld cap and nowhere else besides
content.explanation: Scanning from both sides and along the weld, per the scan plan, helps cover the volume and detect flaws of different orientations.
distractors: A single point does not cover the weld volume.
Coverage requires moving the probe along the weld.
Only scanning the cap misses the weld volume.

content.stem: Focusing and beam control in phased array can improve the ability to:
options: Separate closely spaced reflectors
Change the metal's sound velocity
Do away with the need for couplant
Strip out the metal attenuation
content.explanation: Better beam control improves resolution, helping distinguish reflectors that are close together. It does not change material properties.
distractors: Material velocity is a property of the part, not changed by focusing.
Couplant is still required.
Attenuation is a material property that focusing does not remove.

content.stem: To tie data to position along a scan, phased array often uses an:
options: Encoder
Eraser
Lighter
A ruler
content.explanation: A position encoder records where each scan line was taken so the data maps to the part, enabling encoded imaging and coverage checks.
distractors: An eraser is not a position device.
An illuminator is for viewing radiographs, not encoding position.
A hand ruler does not log scan position automatically; an encoder does.

content.stem: Besides delays, focal laws can vary the relative element amplitudes, a technique called:
options: Apodization
Beam steering
Gain control
Depth focusing
content.explanation: Apodization adjusts element excitation amplitudes across the aperture to shape the beam and reduce side lobes. It is part of the focal-law definition.
distractors: Beam steering sets the angle by delays, not the element amplitudes.
Gain control scales the whole signal, not amplitudes across the aperture.
Depth focusing uses delays for focus, not amplitude weighting.

content.stem: Stepping the active aperture along the array effectively creates a:
options: Moving virtual probe along the array length
A second real probe fixed beside the array
A second fixed-angle wedge bonded beside it
A single static element firing by itself
content.explanation: Selecting different element groups in turn moves the effective beam along the array, like a virtual probe scanning without physical motion.
distractors: No second physical probe is created; it is the same array.
The same array is reused electronically; no second wedge is added.
Stepping the aperture moves a virtual probe; it is not one static element.

content.stem: Phased array is widely used on welds because it can:
options: Cover the weld volume with multiple angles and imaging
Cover only the weld surface right at the top cap face
Work without coupling the probe onto the part at all
See through any thickness with no attenuation loss
content.explanation: Multiple angles and imaging from compact probe positions make phased array effective for volumetric weld inspection, within its physical limits.
distractors: Phased array inspects the volume, not only the surface.
Access to couple the probe is still required.
Thickness and attenuation still limit penetration.

content.stem: Analyzing the recorded images and sizing flaws to acceptance criteria is generally the job of a:
options: Level II or III
A Level I hand
The probe maker
Software seller
content.explanation: A Level I acquires and records valid data; analyzing images, sizing flaws, and evaluating to the code are Level II or higher responsibilities.
distractors: Analysis and evaluation are above the Level I scope.
The probe manufacturer supplies hardware, not the evaluation.
The software vendor supplies tools, not the inspection evaluation.

content.stem: Which statement about phased array fundamentals is correct?
options: A multi-element array is timed to steer and focus the beam electronically, using the same ultrasonic physics as conventional UT
A phased array fires one fixed beam straight down from a single element and cannot be steered to any other angle at all
Phased array runs fully dry with no couplant at all, since its many elements drive the sound straight across the open air gap
A phased array probe carries just one single fixed element, steered to each angle only by tilting the entire probe over by hand
content.explanation: Phased array times many elements to steer and focus the ultrasonic beam, producing multiple angles and images while obeying the same physics as conventional UT.
distractors: A phased array uses many elements timed to steer the beam to many angles.
Couplant is still required to transmit the sound.
A phased array probe has many elements, not one.

content.stem: The center-to-center spacing between array elements is called the:
options: Pitch
Gain
Gate
Skip
content.explanation: Pitch is the element spacing. It strongly affects steering range and grating lobes, so it is a key probe parameter.
distractors: Gain is an amplitude setting, not element spacing.
A gate is a time window on the display, not element spacing.
Skip is an angle-beam path term, not element spacing.

content.stem: A smaller element pitch (relative to wavelength) generally:
options: Reduces grating lobes and allows wider steering
Raises the grating lobes and narrows the steering
Does away with the need for any focal laws at all
Drops the probe operating frequency by itself
content.explanation: Finer pitch keeps element spacing small compared with the wavelength, suppressing grating lobes and allowing the beam to be steered over a wider range.
distractors: Finer pitch reduces, not increases, grating lobes.
Focal laws are still required regardless of pitch.
Pitch is a geometry parameter; it does not set the frequency.

content.stem: The most common phased array probe for weld inspection is a:
options: Linear array (a single row of elements)
Just a single-element conventional probe
An annular concentric-ring array probe
A plain single fixed-angle wedge probe
content.explanation: A 1D linear array, a row of elements, is the common choice for weld scanning, steering and focusing in the plane across the weld.
distractors: A single-element probe is conventional UT, not phased array.
Annular arrays focus on axis; linear arrays are standard for welds.
A fixed-angle conventional wedge probe is not a phased array.

content.stem: The active aperture of a linear array is the:
options: Group of elements fired together for a beam
The elevation height across the elements
The couplant film thickness under the probe
The cable connector on the probe lead end
content.explanation: The active aperture is the set of elements used for one focal law. Its size affects focusing and beam spread.
distractors: The elevation height is the passive aperture, not the active aperture.
Couplant thickness is not the aperture.
The cable connector is hardware, not the aperture.

content.stem: The element dimension perpendicular to the steering direction is the:
options: Passive aperture (elevation)
The active aperture itself
The element pitch spacing only
The chosen focal depth value
content.explanation: The passive aperture (elevation) is fixed by the element height and sets beam spread in the non-steered plane.
distractors: The active aperture is the fired element group, not the elevation.
Pitch is the element spacing, not the elevation.
Focal depth is a focusing setting, not a probe dimension.

content.stem: An annular array (concentric rings) is used mainly to:
options: Focus a straight beam at different depths on axis
Steer the beam out to very large off-axis angles
Sweep a wide fan of angles straight across a weld
Run a stepped linear scan along the array length
content.explanation: Annular arrays focus along the central axis at selectable depths but do not steer in angle, useful for straight-beam depth focusing.
distractors: Annular arrays focus on axis; they do not steer to large angles.
Angle sweeping is a sectorial linear-array scan, not an annular array.
Stepping along the array is a linear scan, done with a linear array.

content.stem: A matrix (2D) array differs from a linear array because it can:
options: Steer and focus in two planes
Only steer in one single plane
Focus along one single axis only
Reach only the near-surface layer
content.explanation: A 2D matrix array has elements in rows and columns, allowing beam control in two planes, at the cost of more channels and complexity.
distractors: Two-plane control is exactly what distinguishes it from a 1D linear array.
A matrix array focuses in two planes, not one axis.
It is volumetric, not limited to the near surface.

content.stem: An angle wedge on a phased array probe is used to:
options: Refract the beam to the desired angles in the part
Cool the array elements down during the long scan
Store the scan data taken from each fired beam
Damp the array elements down to shorten each pulse
content.explanation: The wedge sets a refraction path so the steered beams enter the part at the required angles, and it provides standoff. Its velocity and angle are entered in the setup.
distractors: The wedge does not cool the elements.
Data storage is an instrument function, not the wedge.
Damping is done by the backing material, not the angle wedge.

content.stem: Key wedge parameters entered into the setup include the wedge velocity and the:
options: Wedge angle and probe-to-wedge delay
The couplant viscosity used under it
The base material grain size value
The display screen refresh rate set
content.explanation: The instrument needs the wedge velocity, wedge angle, and element-to-wedge delay to compute correct refracted angles and beam paths.
distractors: Couplant viscosity is not a wedge setup parameter.
Grain size is a material property, not a wedge parameter entered in the setup.
Display refresh rate is unrelated to the wedge setup.

content.stem: A dual-array transmit-receive longitudinal (TRL) probe is often chosen for:
options: Coarse-grained or clad materials with high noise
Thin clean plate and nothing harder than that
Standing in for the position encoder on the rig
Doing away with the need to calibrate at all
content.explanation: TRL probes use separate transmit and receive arrays and a longitudinal mode to improve signal-to-noise in attenuative or coarse-grained materials such as austenitic welds and cladding.
distractors: TRL is aimed at difficult, noisy materials, not only thin clean plate.
A TRL probe does not replace the encoder.
Calibration is still required with a TRL probe.

content.stem: A phased array instrument drives the elements using its:
options: Pulser and receiver channels
One single conventional channel
One shared timing oscillator
A bank of hand toggle switches
content.explanation: The instrument provides many pulser and receiver channels (or multiplexes them) to fire and read the elements with the programmed delays.
distractors: A single conventional channel cannot independently time many elements.
Independent element timing needs many channels, not one oscillator.
Elements are driven by electronic channels, not hand switches.

content.stem: Probe frequency is selected mainly to balance:
options: Resolution against penetration for the material and thickness
Scan speed against the stored file size for the entire job
Wedge angle against the couplant type chosen for the job
Gate width against the receiver gain set on the instrument
content.explanation: Higher frequency improves resolution but penetrates less; the choice suits the material, thickness, and flaws of interest, per the procedure.
distractors: Scan speed and file size are acquisition trade-offs, not what probe frequency balances.
Wedge angle and couplant are separate choices, not the frequency trade-off.
Gate width and gain are display and sensitivity settings, not the frequency trade-off.

content.stem: A position encoder is connected so the instrument can:
options: Tie each scan line to its position on the part
Focus each beam electronically by itself
Generate the focal-law delay set all by itself
Set the reference sensitivity level by itself
content.explanation: The encoder reports probe position so data maps to the part, enabling encoded images and coverage verification.
distractors: Focusing is done by the focal laws, not the encoder.
Focal laws are computed in software, not by the encoder.
Reference sensitivity is set during calibration, not by the encoder.

content.stem: A scanner or manipulator is used to:
options: Hold the probe and carry the encoder along the scan
Set the accept and reject criteria for the entire job
Stand in for the entire acquisition instrument itself
Build the entire focal-law set by itself each time
content.explanation: A scanner holds the probe at a fixed offset and moves it along the weld with the encoder, giving repeatable, position-tracked data.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the scanner.
The scanner positions the probe; it does not replace the instrument.
Focal laws are generated in software, not by the scanner.

content.stem: A probe with several dead (non-functioning) elements can:
options: Degrade the beam and should be checked and addressed
Improve the beam shape sharply across the entire scan
Sharpen the focus right down at every test depth
Be safely ignored for the entire rest of the scan job
content.explanation: Dead elements distort the aperture and beam, lowering sensitivity and image quality, so element integrity is checked and failed probes are repaired or replaced.
distractors: Dead elements degrade, not improve, the beam.
Dead elements distort the aperture; they do not sharpen the focus.
Dead elements affect results and should not be ignored.

content.stem: The probe and wedge contact faces should be:
options: Kept clean and protected from wear and damage
Roughened with coarse grit paper before each use
Scratched up on purpose to help coupling
Left dirty between the jobs to save a little time
content.explanation: A worn or fouled contact face degrades coupling and the beam, so faces are kept clean, inspected, and protected.
distractors: Roughening the contact face harms coupling and the beam.
Scratching the face harms coupling.
A dirty face degrades coupling.

content.stem: Phased array cables and connectors should be handled carefully because:
options: Damaged conductors can disable elements or add noise
They set the material velocity used right in the part
They store the entire focal-law set used for the scan
They build the focal-law set on their own each time
content.explanation: The multi-conductor cable carries each element's signal, so damage can drop elements or add noise, degrading data. Cables are protected and inspected.
distractors: Cables do not set material velocity.
Cables carry signals; the instrument stores the focal laws.
Cables carry signals; the software generates the focal laws.

content.stem: A larger active aperture generally allows:
options: A longer near field and focusing deeper into the part
Focusing only at the near-surface layer of the part
Doing away with the angle wedge altogether on the probe
A lower material sound velocity right through the part
content.explanation: A larger aperture extends the near field, allowing effective focusing at greater depth. Aperture is chosen for the depth of interest.
distractors: A larger aperture focuses deeper, not only at the surface.
Aperture size does not remove the need for a wedge.
Aperture does not change material velocity.

content.stem: In a water-coupled (immersion) phased array setup, the water provides the:
options: Couplant path between the probe and the part
The electrical drive power to the probe array
The focal-law delay set used for each beam
The accept and reject criteria for the job
content.explanation: Immersion uses a water path to transmit sound into the part, with the water-path time accounted for, similar to conventional immersion UT.
distractors: The instrument provides electrical power, not the water.
Focal laws are computed in software, not provided by water.
Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the water path.

content.stem: A matching layer on the array face helps:
options: Transmit sound efficiently between the elements and the wedge or part
Hold the firing delay timing steady across the entire element row set
Store all the scan data taken from each fired beam over the entire job
Steer the beam right out to the larger angles set in the focal law
content.explanation: The matching layer improves acoustic energy transfer from the piezo elements into the wedge or part, similar in purpose to a conventional probe wear face.
distractors: Delays are set electronically per element, not by the matching layer.
It does not store data.
Steering is done by the focal-law delays, not by the matching layer.

content.stem: Selecting a phased array probe and wedge is based mainly on the:
options: Material, thickness, geometry, and angles required
The printed color of the probe cable lead jacket
The operator's own favourite probe brand name on hand
The ambient light level around the inspection bay
content.explanation: The probe frequency, element count, pitch, and wedge are chosen to achieve the required angles and coverage for the material and thickness, per the procedure.
distractors: Cable color does not drive probe selection.
Brand preference is not the technical basis for selection.
Ambient lighting is irrelevant to probe selection.

content.stem: Narrow individual elements help the array:
options: Steer over a wider angular range
Steer dead straight ahead only
Do away with the angle wedge fully
Cancel the material attenuation
content.explanation: Narrower elements have wider individual directivity, supporting steering over a larger angular range before sensitivity falls.
distractors: Narrow elements widen, not restrict, the steering range.
Element width does not remove the need for a wedge.
Element width does not remove material attenuation.

content.stem: The total number of elements and the pitch together set the:
options: Overall probe (array) length
The set material sound velocity
The couplant viscosity used
The accept and reject criteria
content.explanation: Array length equals element count times pitch (approximately), which constrains the apertures and coverage available.
distractors: Material velocity is a property of the part, not the probe length.
Couplant viscosity is unrelated to array length.
Acceptance criteria come from the code.

content.stem: On the instrument, a gate is used to:
options: Select a time or depth window for monitoring signals
Set the firing delay timing for one entire steered beam
Store all the scan data from each beam that is fired
Drive the firing power out to the entire probe array
content.explanation: Gates define time or depth windows where the instrument measures amplitude and position, used during calibration and acquisition.
distractors: Beam timing comes from the focal law, not a gate.
A gate selects a window; it does not store the data.
A gate does not power the probe.

content.stem: An instrument's focal-law capacity limits the:
options: Number of beams (angles or positions) it can produce
The material velocity used right through the test part
The couplant gel chosen for the entire scanning job
The full length of the weld that is being scanned
content.explanation: The instrument can store and fire a finite number of focal laws, which bounds how many angles or aperture positions a setup can use.
distractors: Material velocity is a part property, not set by focal-law capacity.
Couplant choice is independent of focal-law capacity.
Weld length is not set by focal-law capacity.

content.stem: Phased array instruments store encoded data so that:
options: Scans can be reviewed and reported later
No written records are needed for the job
The probe face never wears out at all over time
The calibration step can be skipped entirely
content.explanation: Stored data files allow later review, analysis, and reporting, supporting traceability. Calibration and probe care are still required.
distractors: Records are required, not eliminated, by data storage.
Storing data does not prevent probe wear.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: Dropping or knocking a phased array probe can:
options: Crack elements or the wear face and degrade performance
Improve the sensitivity right across the entire scan job
Run a full self-test on all the array elements at once
Calibrate the entire probe and wedge by itself each time
content.explanation: Impact can damage elements or the face, causing dead elements or coupling loss, so probes are handled and stored carefully.
distractors: Impact damage degrades, not improves, sensitivity.
Impact can damage elements; it does not run a self-test.
Impact does not calibrate the probe.

content.stem: A worn wedge changes the:
options: Refracted angles and beam exit point, requiring re-verification
Material sound velocity of the part being scanned right through
Accept and reject criteria laid down for the entire inspection job
Encoder step resolution measured along the entire scan line
content.explanation: Wedge wear shifts the standoff and angles, so wedges are checked and the setup re-verified, since the beam exit and angles depend on wedge geometry.
distractors: Wedge wear does not change the part's material velocity.
Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the wedge.
Encoder resolution is a separate hardware property.

content.stem: During encoded scanning, a steady couplant supply (such as a water feed) helps:
options: Maintain consistent coupling along the scan
Set the focal-law delay timing for each beam
Power the entire acquisition instrument up
Define the accept and reject criteria used
content.explanation: Consistent couplant prevents coupling loss and data dropout as the probe moves, improving data quality.
distractors: Couplant does not set focal laws.
Couplant does not power the instrument.
Couplant does not define acceptance criteria.

content.stem: Before scanning, element integrity can be verified with the instrument's:
options: Element (dead-element) check function
The backwall echo loss alarm setting
The signal gate threshold level setting
The acceptance criteria lookup table
content.explanation: Many instruments have an element check that shows weak or dead elements, so a faulty probe is caught before acquiring data.
distractors: A backwall echo alarm flags loss of signal, not individual dead elements.
A gate threshold triggers on signal level; it does not test each element.
Acceptance criteria are unrelated to the element check.

content.stem: Compared with a linear array, a matrix array generally requires:
options: More channels and a more complex setup
No acquisition instrument present at all
No focal-law delay set at all
Far fewer elements than a plain linear one
content.explanation: Two-plane control needs more elements and channels and a more involved setup, which is why linear arrays are used where one-plane control suffices.
distractors: An instrument is still required.
Focal laws are still required.
A matrix array has more elements and channels, not fewer.

content.stem: With probes and equipment, the Level I technician is expected to:
options: Set up, inspect, and operate the equipment per the procedure under direction
Design the entire multi-element array probe from scratch by itself
Set the regulatory and code requirements for the entire inspection site
Write and approve the inspection technique for the entire site to use
content.explanation: A Level I assembles, checks, and operates the equipment per the procedure; probe design, regulation, and technique approval are higher-level functions.
distractors: Designing the probe is not a Level I function.
Setting regulatory requirements is not a Level I function.
Approving the technique is above the Level I.

content.stem: A bent or dirty probe connector can cause:
options: Intermittent or dead elements in the data
A higher material velocity right in the part
A brand-new focal law to appear by itself
Better penetration deep into the test part
content.explanation: Poor connector contact interrupts element signals, mimicking dead elements, so connectors are kept clean and undamaged.
distractors: Connector condition does not change material velocity.
A connector fault does not create a focal law.
A bad connector degrades, not improves, results.

content.stem: Which statement about phased array probes and equipment is correct?
options: A multi-element array on a wedge, driven by a multi-channel instrument with an encoder, is set up and operated per the procedure
A phased array probe holds just one single fixed element and is steered to each angle only by tilting it over by hand on the part
An angle wedge is never needed for any angle-beam work, since the bare array alone makes every refracted angle by itself
Focal laws are never needed to form a beam, since the elements just fire all at once together with no delay timing at all
content.explanation: Phased array uses a multi-element array, usually on a wedge, driven by a multi-channel instrument and tracked by an encoder, all set up and operated to the procedure.
distractors: A phased array probe has many elements, not one.
Angle-beam work uses a wedge to set the refracted angles.
Focal laws are required to form each beam.

content.stem: A focal law is best described as the:
options: Set of element time delays (and amplitudes) that defines one beam
The accept and reject criterion the code lays down for a given flaw
A reference sensitivity gain level set once on the instrument unit
A gate position window placed at one spot on the display sweep
content.explanation: Each focal law is a table of per-element delays, and often amplitudes, that produces a specific angle and focus. One law makes one beam.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not a focal law.
Reference sensitivity is a gain setting, not the per-element delay set.
A gate position is a display window, not the beam-defining delays.

content.stem: To steer the beam to an angle, the elements are fired with a:
options: Progressive delay ramp across the array
One single pulse fired across all at once
A random scatter of element delay times
No element delay timing applied at all
content.explanation: A steadily increasing delay from one side of the aperture to the other tilts the combined wavefront, steering the beam to the chosen angle.
distractors: Firing all elements at once gives a straight, unsteered beam.
Random delays would not form a coherent steered beam.
With no delays the beam is not steered.

content.stem: To focus the beam at a depth, the firing pattern is:
options: Curved, so the wavefronts converge at the focal point
Flat, with the same equal timing on each element
Reversed in a random element order on each shot
Set entirely by the couplant film held below the probe
content.explanation: A curved (parabolic) delay pattern fires outer and inner elements at different times so the wavefront converges at the focal depth.
distractors: A flat (equal) timing gives an unfocused beam.
Random reversal would not focus the beam.
Couplant transmits sound; it does not set the focusing delays.

content.stem: A focal law can:
options: Steer and focus the beam at the same time
Only ever steer the beam, and never once focus
Only ever focus the beam, and never once steer
Do neither one of the two at any point
content.explanation: Combining a steering ramp with a focusing curve in the delays sets both the angle and the focal depth of a single beam.
distractors: A focal law can also focus, not only steer.
A focal law can also steer, not only focus.
A focal law produces a defined beam, doing at least one of these.

content.stem: For a sectorial (S) scan, the focal-law set is defined by an angle start, angle stop, and:
options: Angle step (increment)
The couplant type used
The encoder resolution
Plain screen brightness
content.explanation: The S-scan sweeps from the start angle to the stop angle in steps; the step size sets the angular resolution and the number of laws.
distractors: Couplant type is not part of the S-scan angle definition.
Encoder resolution sets scan-axis sampling, not the angle increment.
Display brightness is a viewing setting, not an angle parameter.

content.stem: For an electronic linear (E) scan, the focal laws keep the angle fixed and vary the:
options: First element, stepping the aperture along the array
The set material sound velocity right through the part
The couplant temperature under the moving probe
The gate measurement window width on the display
content.explanation: An E-scan holds the angle and focus and moves the active aperture element by element along the array, scanning without physical motion.
distractors: Material velocity is a part property, not a stepped focal-law parameter.
Couplant temperature is not what an E-scan steps.
Gate width is a measurement window, not what an E-scan steps.

content.stem: The number of elements used in each focal law is the:
options: Active aperture for that beam
The fixed element pitch value
The display gate width window
The angle-beam skip distance
content.explanation: Each law specifies how many elements form the aperture; larger apertures focus deeper and narrow the beam, within limits.
distractors: Pitch is the fixed element spacing, not the per-law aperture.
Gate width is a display window, not the aperture.
Skip distance is an angle-beam path term, not the aperture.

content.stem: Electronic focusing is only effective:
options: Within the near field of the aperture
Out beyond the near field, at any depth
Only at the very part surface itself
Only out in the open air above the part
content.explanation: Focusing can place the focal point only within the near-field length of the aperture; beyond that the beam diverges and cannot be focused.
distractors: Focusing cannot be achieved beyond the near field.
Focusing is not limited to the surface; it works through the near field.
Focusing applies in the part, not in air.

content.stem: Focal laws are normally generated by:
options: Software from the probe, wedge, and material inputs
Hand-soldering a separate delay line for each element
The couplant supplier listed on the gel data sheet
The encoder wheel rolling along the part surface
content.explanation: The instrument or software computes the delays from the probe geometry, wedge, material velocity, and the desired angles and focus.
distractors: Delays are computed electronically, not hand-soldered.
The couplant supplier does not generate focal laws.
The encoder reports position; it does not generate focal laws.

content.stem: If the wedge velocity or angle is entered incorrectly, the focal laws will:
options: Produce incorrect refracted angles and beam positions
Stay completely unaffected by the wrong wedge input
Improve the angle accuracy across the entire sweep
Raise the probe operating frequency by itself
content.explanation: The computed delays depend on the wedge and material inputs, so wrong values give wrong angles and mislocated reflectors, which is why inputs are verified.
distractors: Incorrect inputs do affect the resulting beams.
Wrong inputs degrade, not improve, accuracy.
Inputs do not change the probe frequency.

content.stem: Grating lobes are most associated with:
options: Element pitch that is large relative to the wavelength
An element pitch far smaller than the sound wavelength
A clean couplant film held under the moving probe face
A short probe cable running back to the instrument unit
content.explanation: When pitch is large compared with the wavelength, extra (grating) lobes appear off the main beam and can cause spurious indications.
distractors: A small pitch suppresses grating lobes.
Couplant cleanliness does not cause grating lobes.
Cable length does not cause grating lobes.

content.stem: As the steering angle increases toward the array limits, sensitivity generally:
options: Decreases
Climbs up
Holds set
Goes huge
content.explanation: Element directivity falls off with angle, so steered beams at extreme angles lose sensitivity, which is why steering ranges are bounded in the setup.
distractors: Sensitivity falls, rather than rising without limit, at extreme angles.
Sensitivity changes with steering angle; it is not constant.
Sensitivity does not become infinite.

content.stem: Using a smaller angle step in an S-scan gives:
options: Finer angular sampling but more focal laws
Coarser angular sampling over the sweep
Fewer total beams formed over the sweep
A lower probe operating frequency set
content.explanation: A smaller step samples more angles, improving angular detail at the cost of more focal laws and data, balanced against acquisition speed.
distractors: A smaller step gives finer, not coarser, sampling.
A smaller step gives more, not fewer, beams.
Step size does not change the frequency.

content.stem: Apodization in a focal law adjusts element:
options: Amplitudes across the aperture to shape the beam
Velocities across the entire fired aperture group
Frequencies across the entire fired aperture group
Physical positions of the fixed elements in the row
content.explanation: Apodization weights the excitation amplitudes across the aperture to reduce side lobes and shape the beam, complementing the delay pattern.
distractors: Element velocities are not changed by apodization.
Apodization weights amplitudes; it does not change element frequency.
Apodization does not move the elements; their positions are fixed.

content.stem: The focal depth in a focal law sets:
options: Where the beam is concentrated for best response
The couplant film thickness under the probe face
The probe operating frequency set for the job
The accept and reject criteria taken from the code
content.explanation: Focal depth places the focal point where the best resolution and sensitivity are wanted, within the near-field limit.
distractors: Focal depth does not set couplant thickness.
Focal depth does not set probe frequency.
Acceptance criteria come from the code.

content.stem: If no focusing is applied, the beam is:
options: Unfocused and diverges with depth
Focused sharply at every test depth
Steered out to all angles at once
Switched fully off and silent
content.explanation: With equal delays (no focusing curve), the beam is unfocused and spreads with depth, giving lower resolution than a focused beam.
distractors: Without a focusing curve the beam is not focused.
One law gives one angle, not every angle at once.
An unfocused beam is still active, not off.

content.stem: The number of focal laws in a setup equals the number of:
options: Beams (angles or aperture positions)
The couplant types kept in the kit
Cables fitted on the probe lead
Operators working on the crew
content.explanation: Each beam needs its own focal law, so an S-scan with many angles or an E-scan with many positions uses many laws.
distractors: Couplant types are not counted as focal laws.
Cables are not counted as focal laws.
Operators are not focal laws.

content.stem: Focusing options such as true depth, half path, and projection differ in:
options: How the focal distance is defined relative to the beam path
Which couplant gel is used under the moving probe face plate
How many elements are fired in the active aperture group
Which display color palette is chosen on the screen
content.explanation: These focusing modes set the focal point relative to depth, sound path, or a projected plane, chosen to suit the inspection. The principle is the same focusing law.
distractors: The couplant choice does not define these focusing modes.
Element count affects aperture, not which focusing reference is used.
The display palette is a viewing setting, not a focusing mode.

content.stem: A larger active aperture generally produces a:
options: Narrower beam with less spread
A wider, far more divergent beam
A beam that needs no delays now
A lower set material velocity
content.explanation: A larger aperture narrows the beam and extends the near field, improving focusing and resolution, within steering limits.
distractors: A larger aperture narrows, not widens, the beam.
Delays are still required to steer and focus.
Aperture does not change material velocity.

content.stem: Accurate beam forming depends on the instrument's:
options: Precise control of the element timing (delays)
The overall size of the couplant reservoir tank
The count of saved setups stored on the unit
The brightness level set on the display screen
content.explanation: The delays must be applied precisely for the wavefronts to combine correctly; timing errors distort the beam and mislocate reflectors.
distractors: Couplant reservoir size does not affect beam forming.
How many setups are stored does not affect beam forming.
Display brightness does not affect the delays.

content.stem: After generating focal laws, the actual refracted angles should be:
options: Verified on a reference block
Assumed right with no real check
Left fully ignored each time
Set by the couplant gel alone
content.explanation: The produced angles are verified on a calibration block so the real beam matches the intended setup before scanning.
distractors: Angles are verified, not assumed.
Verification is required, not ignored.
Couplant does not set the refracted angles.

content.stem: The angular sweep range of an S-scan is limited by the:
options: Probe and wedge design (steering capability)
The couplant type held under the moving probe
The encoder step size set along the scan line
The stored data file format chosen for the job
content.explanation: How far the beam can be steered with adequate sensitivity depends on the element pitch, frequency, and wedge, so the usable sweep is bounded.
distractors: Couplant type does not limit the sweep range.
Encoder step sets scan-axis sampling, not the angular sweep range.
The data file format does not limit the sweep range.

content.stem: The material velocity entered in the setup affects the focal laws because it changes the:
options: Refraction and the computed beam paths
The display color palette on the screen
The couplant viscosity under the probe
The probe scanning speed along the weld
content.explanation: Velocity governs refraction and time-to-depth, so an incorrect velocity gives wrong angles and depths, which is why it is set correctly.
distractors: Velocity changes refraction, not the display palette.
Velocity does not change couplant viscosity.
Velocity does not change the scan speed.

content.stem: Side lobes and grating lobes matter because they can:
options: Produce spurious indications off the main beam
Sharpen and improve the main beam shape itself
Add useful penetration far deeper into the part
Take the place of the focal-law set entirely
content.explanation: Energy outside the main beam can reflect off geometry or flaws and appear as false signals, so probe design and apodization limit them.
distractors: These lobes degrade, not improve, the main beam.
They do not increase useful penetration.
They are artifacts, not a replacement for focal laws.

content.stem: Using many focal laws (large sweeps, fine steps) tends to:
options: Slow the acquisition rate
Speed it up with no limit
Drop the position encoder
End all need to calibrate
content.explanation: More beams per position mean more firing and processing, lowering the achievable scan speed, which is balanced against coverage and resolution.
distractors: More laws slow, not speed, acquisition.
More laws do not remove the encoder.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: The generated focal laws are stored as part of the:
options: Setup or configuration file
The acceptance criteria set
The couplant gel data sheet
The position encoder lead
content.explanation: The setup file holds the focal laws, gains, and gates so the configuration can be reused and verified. A Level I loads and verifies it.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are separate from the setup file.
The couplant data sheet does not hold focal laws.
The encoder cable carries position signals, not the focal laws.

content.stem: Compensating gain so equal reflectors read the same at all depths and angles is done by:
options: Time-corrected and angle-corrected gain, applied to the laws
Swapping the couplant gel out for a thicker grade mid-scan
Adding extra length onto the probe cable run to the unit
Renaming the probe entry in the saved setup file each time
content.explanation: TCG and ACG add depth- and angle-dependent gain so a reference reflector gives a consistent amplitude across the focal laws, set during calibration.
distractors: Couplant changes do not provide depth and angle gain correction.
Cable length does not correct gain.
Renaming the probe does not correct gain.

content.stem: Across an S-scan sweep, the beam exit point on the wedge:
options: Can shift with angle, which the setup accounts for
Never shifts at any point across the angular sweep
Sets the accept and reject criteria for the job
Drives power to the entire acquisition instrument
content.explanation: Different angles can exit at slightly different points and times; the wedge and delay parameters account for this so positions are computed correctly.
distractors: The exit can shift with angle; it is not perfectly fixed.
Beam exit does not set acceptance criteria.
Beam exit does not power the instrument.

content.stem: Focusing improves resolution mainly by:
options: Narrowing the beam at the focal depth
Widening the beam at every test depth
Raising the set material velocity used
Taking the angle wedge off the probe
content.explanation: A narrower focused beam separates close reflectors better at the focal depth, improving lateral resolution there.
distractors: Focusing narrows the beam at the focus, not widens it everywhere.
Focusing does not change material velocity.
Focusing does not remove the wedge.

content.stem: Regarding focal laws, a Level I technician usually:
options: Generates or loads laws from the procedure and verifies them under direction
Derives the new accept and reject criteria for the entire inspection job alone
Designs the entire multi-element array probe from scratch by itself
Writes the governing inspection code for the entire site to follow
content.explanation: A Level I builds or loads the focal laws specified by the procedure and verifies the resulting angles and sensitivity; criteria, probe design, and codes are higher-level.
distractors: Deriving acceptance criteria is above the Level I.
Designing the array is not a Level I task.
Writing the code is above the Level I.

content.stem: Beam steering and focusing are defined by the focal law. Which of these is NOT a focal-law parameter?
options: The couplant used
The steering angle
The active aperture
The focal depth
content.explanation: The focal law is defined by parameters such as the steering angle, active aperture, and focal depth. The couplant transmits sound into the part but is not a focal-law parameter.
distractors: The steering angle, set by the per-element delay ramp, is a focal-law parameter.
The active aperture, the elements fired together, is a focal-law parameter.
The focal depth is a focal-law parameter.

content.stem: Focusing tightly at one depth means reflectors far from that depth may be:
options: Less well resolved there
Resolved better everywhere
Lost in the near dead zone
Wiped out of the data set
content.explanation: A beam focused at one depth diverges away from it, so resolution falls off at other depths, which the setup and depth-of-field choice manage.
distractors: Focusing at one depth does not improve resolution everywhere.
Out-of-focus reflectors are still shown, not lost to the dead zone.
Out-of-focus reflectors still appear in the data.

content.stem: Before acquiring data, the focal-law setup should be:
options: Calibrated and verified on a reference block
Used straight off with no check made at all
Taken as perfect with no checking done at all
Deleted right off before the scan starts
content.explanation: Verifying angles, sensitivity, and depth on a reference block confirms the laws perform as intended before real scanning begins.
distractors: The setup is verified, not used unchecked.
Performance is verified, not assumed.
The setup is kept and used, not deleted.

content.stem: Which statement about focal laws is correct?
options: Per-element delays steer and focus each beam, generated from probe, wedge, and material inputs and verified before scanning
A focal law by itself lays down the accept and reject criteria for the joint, with no reference block check needed before scanning
Electronic focusing works just as well at any depth far beyond the near field, with no real limit on the focal range at all
Grating lobes come up only from an element pitch that is very small next to the sound wavelength, never from a large pitch at all
content.explanation: Focal laws are the per-element delay and amplitude tables that steer and focus each beam; they come from the setup inputs, are limited by the near field, and are verified before use.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not focal laws.
Focusing is limited to within the near field.
Grating lobes come from large, not small, pitch.

content.stem: The basic waveform underlying every phased array beam is the:
options: A-scan (amplitude versus time)
A plan-view C-scan image only
An S-scan angular fan view only
A side-view depth cross-section
content.explanation: Each beam still produces an A-scan of amplitude versus time. The image views are built from many A-scans.
distractors: A C-scan is a plan-view image built from A-scans, not the basic waveform.
An S-scan is a built image, not the basic waveform.
A side view is built from A-scans, not the basic waveform itself.

content.stem: A sectorial (S) scan displays:
options: A fan of angles from one probe position as a cross-section
Just one single A-scan trace shown by itself with nothing else
A plan top-view mapping out the entire scanned area at once
A stepped fixed-angle image run along the array length
content.explanation: The S-scan shows reflectors across a swept range of angles from one position, giving a cross-sectional fan image, a signature phased array view.
distractors: An S-scan shows many angles, not a single A-scan.
A plan view over an area is a C-scan, not an S-scan.
Stepping a fixed angle along the array is an E-scan, not an S-scan.

content.stem: An electronic linear (E) scan image is produced by:
options: Stepping a fixed-angle aperture along the array
Sweeping many angles out from one fixed aperture
Holding one fixed angle on a single fixed spot
Tilting the probe over by hand for each scan line
content.explanation: An E-scan keeps the angle constant and moves the aperture along the array, imaging a strip without physical probe motion.
distractors: Sweeping angles from one aperture is the S-scan, not the E-scan.
Holding one angle on one spot is not a scan along the array.
An E-scan steps electronically, not by hand-tilting the probe.

content.stem: A cross-sectional view that plots depth against position along the scan is most useful for showing:
options: How a reflector's depth changes along the scan
The plan-view extent across the entire scan area
A single beam's raw A-scan waveform by itself
The amplitude held within one fixed gate window
content.explanation: A depth-versus-position cross-section (a side view) shows how a reflector's depth varies along the scan direction. Plan-view extent comes from a top view, and a single waveform is the A-scan.
distractors: The plan-view extent over an area is shown by a top (plan) view, not a depth cross-section.
A single beam's waveform is the A-scan, not a cross-sectional view.
A single gated amplitude is not a depth-versus-position cross-section.

content.stem: A C-scan presents a:
options: Plan (top) view mapping amplitude or depth over an area
A single raw A-scan waveform shown by itself only
A fan of swept angles taken from one single fixed position
A side-view depth slice taken straight along the scan line
content.explanation: A C-scan maps a gated value such as amplitude or depth across the scanned area as a top view, helping show the extent of reflectors.
distractors: A single A-scan is the basic waveform, not a C-scan.
A fan of angles from one position is the S-scan.
A depth slice along the scan is a side view, not a C-scan.

content.stem: In phased array image views, color usually represents:
options: Signal amplitude
The couplant type
The set scan speed
The element count
content.explanation: A color palette maps echo amplitude (or sometimes depth), so stronger signals show in different colors, aiding visualization. Evaluation is a higher-level task.
distractors: Color maps amplitude, not the couplant type.
Color maps amplitude, not the scan speed.
Color maps amplitude, not the element count.

content.stem: An encoded scan differs from a free-running (live) scan because it:
options: Links each image line to a recorded position
Cannot be saved off to a file at all afterward
Uses no focal-law delay set at all during it
Needs no couplant on the scanning surface
content.explanation: Encoded scanning records position so the data maps to the part and can be reviewed; free-running shows live images without position records.
distractors: Encoded data is saved with position, not unable to be saved.
Focal laws are still used in encoded scanning.
Couplant is still required.

content.stem: Selecting a point in an S-scan image typically shows the:
options: A-scan for the corresponding beam
The accept and reject criteria table
The entire scan plan layout instead
The full calibration certificate
content.explanation: The image is built from A-scans, so selecting a beam or point recalls its A-scan for closer examination, supporting analysis at the appropriate level.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are not shown by selecting an image point.
Selecting a point recalls its A-scan, not the scan plan.
Selecting a point recalls its A-scan, not the calibration certificate.

content.stem: Top, side, and end views in phased array correspond to different:
options: Projection planes of the volumetric data
Different couplant types in current use
Different probe frequency settings in use
Different receiver gain settings in use
content.explanation: The same volumetric data can be projected as top, side, and end views to see reflectors from different directions.
distractors: These are projection planes, not couplant types.
These are projection planes, not different probe frequencies.
These are projection planes, not gain settings.

content.stem: In a basic (uncorrected) sectorial (S) scan display, one axis represents the swept angle and the other represents:
options: Sound path or depth
Couplant viscosity
The set gain level
The scan position
content.explanation: In the basic uncorrected sectorial display, reflectors are plotted by swept angle and sound path (or depth). A corrected (true-view) S-scan instead plots reflectors in spatial coordinates, horizontal distance and depth, with the angle implicit.
distractors: Couplant viscosity is not a display axis.
Gain is a sensitivity setting, not an S-scan axis.
Scan-axis position is the encoded-scan axis, not the S-scan's second (depth) axis.

content.stem: The image views are built from data measured within the:
options: Gates set on the signals
A couplant reservoir tank
The solid wedge body
The outer probe case
content.explanation: Gates select the time or depth ranges whose amplitude and position feed the C-scan and other views, so gate setup affects the imaging.
distractors: The couplant reservoir does not produce image data.
The wedge body is hardware; image data comes from the gated signals.
The probe case does not produce image data.

content.stem: An end view of the scanned volume presents the reflectors as if:
options: Looking along the weld axis, from the end
Looking straight down from above the joint
Looking from the side along the entire scan
Shown as one single raw A-scan waveform
content.explanation: An end view projects the data as if looking along the weld axis, from the end, complementing the side and top views.
distractors: Looking from directly above is a top (plan) view, not an end view.
Looking from the side along the scan is a side view, not an end view.
A single A-scan is one beam's waveform, not an end view.

content.stem: Image views help the inspection by:
options: Showing reflector position and extent at a glance
Setting the accept and reject criteria for the work
Standing in for the entire calibration step each time
Doing away with the need for full scan coverage
content.explanation: Images make it easier to see where reflectors are and how they extend, aiding review. Criteria, calibration, and coverage are still required.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not the image view.
Images do not replace calibration.
Coverage is still required regardless of imaging.

content.stem: A free-running display is useful for:
options: Setup and quick checks before encoded recording
Keeping the permanent records for the entire job
Standing in for the written scan plan itself
Doing away with the entire focal-law set
content.explanation: Live imaging helps position the probe and verify coupling and response; encoded recording is used for the documented inspection.
distractors: Permanent records come from encoded scanning, not the live view.
The live view does not replace the scan plan.
Focal laws are still used in live imaging.

content.stem: A reflector shown in the color mapped to high amplitude indicates a:
options: Strong returning signal at that point
A weak returning signal at that point
A couplant change right under the probe
A cable fault on the probe lead run
content.explanation: The palette maps stronger echoes to the high-amplitude colors, so that color marks a strong return. Whether it is relevant is judged at a higher level.
distractors: High-amplitude color marks a strong, not weak, signal.
It indicates signal strength, not a couplant change.
It indicates signal strength, not a cable fault.

content.stem: On-screen cursors and readouts let the technician:
options: Read positions and amplitudes from the data
Set the regulatory limits for the entire job
Re-steer the beam out to brand-new angles
Generate a fresh focal-law set on their own
content.explanation: Measurement cursors report depth, position, and amplitude from the recorded data, supporting later analysis. Final evaluation is a higher-level task.
distractors: Regulatory limits are set by the code, not the cursor tools.
Cursors read the data; they do not re-steer the beam.
Cursors read the data; the software generates focal laws.

content.stem: Viewing the A-scan, S-scan, and C-scan together helps:
options: Locate and characterize reflectors more completely
Set the couplant viscosity used for the entire scan
Stand in for the entire position encoder on the rig
Power the entire probe array up by itself each time
content.explanation: Multiple linked views give a fuller picture of a reflector's position and extent, aiding review at the appropriate level.
distractors: Combining views does not set couplant viscosity.
Combining views does not replace the encoder.
Combining views does not power the probe.

content.stem: A volume-corrected (true-depth) view positions reflectors by:
options: Their actual depth and position in the part
Their plain signal amplitude value alone only
The plain order in which they were detected
The receiver gain setting that is in use
content.explanation: Volume correction maps the angled beam data to real part coordinates so reflectors appear at their true depth and location.
distractors: Amplitude is shown by color; the true-depth view places reflectors by position, not amplitude alone.
Detection order does not set the displayed position.
The gain setting does not set the displayed position.

content.stem: One advantage of the S-scan for welds is that a single position can:
options: Insonify the weld with a range of angles at once
Cover only one single fixed angle at a time on it
Skip moving the probe along the entire weld
Do away with the angle wedge on the probe entirely
content.explanation: The angular sweep covers different parts of the weld bevel from one position, though the probe is still moved along the weld for full coverage.
distractors: One fixed angle is the conventional case, not an S-scan.
The probe is still moved along the weld for coverage.
A wedge is still used for angle-beam work.

content.stem: At Level I, recognizing the scan views and identifying signals is expected, while deciding acceptance is:
options: A Level II or III responsibility
Also a routine part of Level I work
Done by the probe array itself
Set by the couplant gel alone
content.explanation: A Level I reads and records the displays and identifies signals; interpreting and accepting or rejecting against the code is a higher-level responsibility.
distractors: Acceptance decisions are above the Level I.
The probe does not decide acceptance.
The couplant does not decide acceptance.

content.stem: A C-scan is especially helpful for showing a reflector's:
options: Length and extent over the scanned area
Its exact metallurgical cause directly
Its precise through-wall height directly
Its exact chemical composition make-up
content.explanation: The plan-view C-scan reveals how far a reflector extends along and across the scan, useful for review. Cause and acceptance are higher-level judgments.
distractors: The metallurgical cause is not read directly from a C-scan.
Through-wall height comes from depth views and higher-level sizing, not the top-view extent.
Chemical composition is not shown by a C-scan.

content.stem: Two cross-sectional views show depth: one plots depth along the scan direction, the other plots depth across the index direction. These are, respectively, the:
options: Side view and the end view
End view and the side view
Top view and the plan view
The A-scan and the S-scan
content.explanation: A depth cross-section along the scan direction is the side view; a depth cross-section across the index direction is the end view. These are descriptive view names, independent of any letter convention.
distractors: The order is reversed: depth along the scan is the side view, and depth across the index is the end view.
A top (plan) view looks from above and is not a depth cross-section.
The A-scan is a single waveform and the S-scan is an angular fan, not depth cross-sections.

content.stem: Poor coupling during a scan typically shows in the views as:
options: Data dropout or low-amplitude regions
Sharper, cleaner images right on screen
A higher set material velocity reading
A brand-new focal law made by itself
content.explanation: Loss of coupling reduces signal, appearing as gaps or weak areas in the imaging, which the technician watches for and corrects.
distractors: Poor coupling degrades, not sharpens, the images.
Coupling loss does not raise material velocity.
Coupling loss does not create a focal law.

content.stem: Combining data from multiple angles or groups into one view is called:
options: Merging (or compounding) the data
Gating a single window in the data
Steering a single beam in the data
Focusing one beam down in the data
content.explanation: Merged or compounded views combine beams to give a clearer composite image, used to aid review.
distractors: Gating selects one window; it does not combine multiple angles.
Steering one beam is not combining several into one view.
Focusing a single beam is not merging several angles.

content.stem: In encoded line scanning, the scan axis is the direction the probe:
options: Moves along (tracked by the encoder)
Is lifted right up away from the part
Is stepped over between the scan passes
Is dipped down into the couplant pot
content.explanation: The scan axis is the encoded travel direction; the index axis is the step offset between lines. Together they map coverage.
distractors: Lifting the probe loses coupling; it is not the scan axis.
Stepping across between passes is the index axis, not the scan axis.
Dipping in couplant is not the scan axis.

content.stem: The color palette and display range are set so that:
options: Relevant signals are clearly visible for review
The couplant gel looks bright and colorful
The probe cable is fully hidden away off screen
The probe array runs a little cooler on the job
content.explanation: Appropriate palette and gain ranges make signals readable in the images, aiding review without saturating or hiding detail.
distractors: The palette is for signals, not couplant appearance.
The palette does not hide the cable.
The palette does not cool the probe.

content.stem: Sweeping angles in an S-scan is useful on a weld because flaws can lie:
options: At different orientations along the bevel
Only ever at one single fixed bevel angle
Only at the outer part surface itself
Only out well beyond the edge of the part
content.explanation: Different angles intersect differently oriented flaws and bevel faces, improving the chance of detection across the weld.
