distractors: Flaws are not all at one orientation, which is why angles are swept.
Phased array detects volumetric, not only surface, flaws.
Flaws of interest are within the part, not outside it.

content.stem: Image positions are only trustworthy if the setup is:
options: Correctly calibrated (velocity, wedge, angles)
Just run flat out at the maximum gain setting
Run with no position encoder fitted on the rig
Fitted with the newest probe array on hand
content.explanation: Reflector positions in the views depend on correct velocity, wedge, and angle calibration; without it, the images mislocate reflectors.
distractors: Maximum gain does not ensure correct positions.
Encoded position requires an encoder, not its absence.
Probe age does not establish correct positions; calibration does.

content.stem: A clean-looking image still requires:
options: That the planned coverage was actually achieved
Nothing more at all to be done beyond the image
Only the most couplant possible on the surface
Only the largest probe array fitted on the rig
content.explanation: Good-looking data over part of the weld does not prove full coverage, so coverage is verified against the scan plan regardless of image quality.
distractors: Coverage verification is still required.
Couplant amount alone does not ensure coverage.
Probe size alone does not ensure coverage.

content.stem: With displays, the Level I technician:
options: Recognizes the views and records the data under direction
Makes the final acceptance call on the welded joint alone
Sets the entire accept and reject criteria for the job alone
Writes the entire inspection procedure for the site to use
content.explanation: A Level I reads and records the views and identifies signals; final acceptance, criteria, and procedures are higher-level responsibilities.
distractors: The final acceptance call is above the Level I.
Setting criteria is above the Level I.
Writing the procedure is above the Level I.

content.stem: Indications from grating lobes, mode conversion, or geometry in the images must be:
options: Recognized as possible artifacts, not assumed to be flaws
Always counted straight off as real flaws to reject
Ignored completely and left out of the report each time
Erased clean out of the recorded data set straight away
content.explanation: Not every indication is a flaw; the technician recognizes possible artifacts so they are not mistaken for defects, with evaluation done at a higher level.
distractors: Not every indication is a flaw.
Indications are reviewed, not ignored.
Data is preserved, not erased.

content.stem: For documentation, the encoded image views are:
options: Saved as data files tied to the part
Discarded soon after a quick look
Kept only in volatile memory store
Left fully unidentified and unlabelled
content.explanation: The saved files, with identification and position, form the inspection record for review and traceability.
distractors: The data files are retained, not discarded.
Files are saved, not kept only in memory.
Files must be identified for traceability.

content.stem: To judge how far a reflector extends along the weld, the most directly useful view is the:
options: C-scan (top view)
The single A-scan
The probe sticker
The couplant chart
content.explanation: The plan-view C-scan shows extent along the weld at a glance, while the A-scan alone shows one beam. Final sizing is a higher-level task.
distractors: A single A-scan shows one beam, not the extent along the weld.
The probe label does not show reflector extent.
A couplant chart does not show reflector extent.

content.stem: Which statement about phased array scan types is correct?
options: A-scans build the S-scan and the cross-section, plan, and end views; encoded scanning ties them to position; reading them is Level I, evaluating them is Level II
The C-scan top view is the single basic waveform behind every beam, and the A-scan is just a plan-view map built from many separate C-scans over an area
An S-scan is taken at one single fixed angle held throughout, and stepping a fixed-angle aperture along the array is what sweeps a full fan of angles instead
Encoded scanning keeps no record of probe position at all, and a plain free-running live view is what ties every image line back to a tracked position on the part
content.explanation: Phased array assembles A-scans into the S-scan and the cross-section, plan, and end views, ties them to position when encoded, and the technician reads and records them while evaluation is a higher-level task.
distractors: The A-scan, not the C-scan, is the basic waveform.
An S-scan sweeps many angles, not one fixed angle.
Encoded scanning is defined by tying data to a recorded position.

content.stem: Velocity calibration sets the instrument so that:
options: Depth and sound-path readings match the known material velocity
The probe array runs a good deal cooler all through the long scan
The couplant gel on the surface lasts a fair bit longer than usual
The probe cable back to the instrument ends up a fair bit shorter
content.explanation: Calibrating velocity on a known block makes the depth and position readings correct for the material, as in conventional UT.
distractors: Velocity calibration does not cool the probe.
It does not affect couplant life.
It does not change the cable.

content.stem: Wedge delay calibration accounts for the time the sound spends:
options: In the wedge before entering the part
In the probe cable lead on the way in
Bouncing off the backwall echo surface
Inside the display software code itself
content.explanation: The wedge delay (zero offset) removes the in-wedge travel time so depths are measured from the part surface, not from the elements.
distractors: Cable delay is small and is folded into the overall zero and delay calibration; it is not the wedge-in time the wedge delay removes.
The wedge delay removes in-wedge travel time; it is not about the backwall echo.
Display software does not add the wedge travel time.

content.stem: Time-corrected gain (TCG) is built so that:
options: Equal reflectors read the same amplitude at different depths
Deeper reflectors always read lower than the shallow ones do
The couplant gel slowly shifts its color across the surface
The probe operating frequency climbs higher as the scan runs
content.explanation: TCG adds depth-dependent gain so an equal reference reflector gives the same amplitude regardless of depth, compensating attenuation and beam spread.
distractors: TCG exists to remove, not keep, the depth-related amplitude drop.
TCG does not change couplant color.
TCG does not change probe frequency.

content.stem: TCG is commonly built using:
options: A reference reflector such as side-drilled holes at several depths
A single shallow surface scratch at just one spot on the block
The couplant reservoir tank sitting up on top of the scanning rig
The range of display palette colors shown across the entire screen
content.explanation: Side-drilled holes at known depths give equal reflectors at increasing sound paths, from which the depth-gain curve is built.
distractors: A single scratch does not give equal reflectors at multiple depths.
The couplant reservoir is not a reference reflector.
The display palette does not provide reference reflectors for TCG.

content.stem: Angle-corrected gain (ACG) compensates for amplitude differences:
options: Across the angles of an S-scan
Between two separate test parts
From the saved data file format
From the operator's own hand
content.explanation: Sensitivity varies with steering angle, so ACG equalizes the response across the sweep using a reference reflector, giving consistent amplitudes.
distractors: ACG corrects across angles, not between unrelated parts.
The data file format does not cause the amplitude variation.
The operator does not cause the angle-dependent variation.

content.stem: Setting the reference sensitivity means adjusting gain so a reference reflector reaches a:
options: Defined screen height (for example a set percent of full screen)
Flat zero amplitude sitting right down on the baseline floor
Whatever random screen height it happens to land at on the day
The very maximum screen height the instrument will ever allow
content.explanation: The reference reflector is brought to a defined amplitude to establish the sensitivity from which scanning gain is referenced.
distractors: A reference is set to a defined height, not zero.
The height is defined, not random.
It is set to a defined level, not simply the maximum.

content.stem: Before calibrating, the technician should confirm that the probe has:
options: No dead or weak elements affecting the aperture
The highest available gain preset dialed in
A bright and colorful couplant gel spread on it
A nicely warmed-up wear face on the front of it
content.explanation: Dead elements distort the beam and calibration, so element integrity is checked first and a faulty probe is replaced.
distractors: A gain preset does not substitute for checking element integrity.
Couplant color is irrelevant to the element check.
Wear-face temperature is not the element check.

content.stem: The actual refracted angles can be verified using:
options: A known radius on a calibration block
The couplant gel data sheet on the rig
The display palette set on the screen
The pulse repetition frequency value set
content.explanation: Reflecting off a machined radius lets the technician confirm the beam exits and refracts at the intended angles before scanning.
distractors: The couplant data sheet does not verify angles.
The display palette does not verify the refracted angles.
The pulse repetition frequency does not verify the refracted angles.

content.stem: Encoder calibration ensures that:
options: Recorded distance matches actual probe travel
The probe array never once wears out over time
The couplant gel always stays perfectly fresh
The display comes out bright and full of color
content.explanation: Moving the encoder a known distance and setting the counts makes the recorded scan position accurate, so images map correctly to the part.
distractors: Encoder calibration does not prevent probe wear.
It does not affect couplant freshness.
It is about position accuracy, not display color.

content.stem: Calibration uses blocks with:
options: Known reflectors such as SDHs, FBHs, notches, or radii
Random unknown surface features dotted about all over it
No machined features cut into the block at all anywhere
Only a plain coat of surface paint brushed over it all
content.explanation: Reference blocks contain known reflectors and dimensions so the setup can be calibrated and verified against the procedure.
distractors: Calibration needs known, not random, features.
A featureless block cannot calibrate reflector response.
Paint alone is not a calibration reflector.

content.stem: Calibration should be done under conditions that match scanning, including:
options: Surface condition and temperature
The ambient room lighting level set
The saved scan data file naming
The chosen display color palette
content.explanation: Because velocity and coupling vary with temperature and surface, calibrating under representative conditions keeps the setup valid during scanning.
distractors: Ambient lighting does not affect ultrasonic calibration validity.
File naming does not affect calibration validity.
The display palette does not affect calibration validity.

content.stem: During calibration, gates are set to:
options: Capture the reference reflector signals for measurement
Hold the firing delay timing for the steered beam set
Build the entire cross-section image view by themselves
Drive the power out to the position encoder on the rig
content.explanation: Gates bracket the reference echoes so their amplitude and position are measured for the velocity, delay, TCG, and sensitivity steps.
distractors: Gates select a signal window; they do not set the beam timing.
Gates select a measurement window; the views are built from A-scans.
Gates do not power the encoder.

content.stem: After building TCG or ACG, the response should be checked:
options: Across the full angular sweep or depth range
At just one single fixed steered angle only
Only along the length of the probe cable lead
Only within the couplant gel layer below it
content.explanation: Verifying that an equal reflector reads consistently across the angles and depths confirms the corrections work over the whole setup.
distractors: Checking one angle does not verify the whole sweep.
The cable is not the response being checked.
The couplant is not the response being checked.

content.stem: When using a stored setup file, the technician should:
options: Load it and verify it on the calibration block before scanning
Trust it straight off with no real check made on it at all first
Delete it right off the unit before the scan even gets started
Rename the entire probe entry in the saved setup file instead
content.explanation: A loaded setup is verified against the reference block so the angles, sensitivity, and depth are confirmed correct before acquiring data.
distractors: A loaded setup is verified, not blindly trusted.
The setup is used, not deleted.
Renaming the probe does not verify the setup.

content.stem: Calibration is rechecked periodically during a job because:
options: Temperature, wear, or drift can change the response
The setup response never once changes over the entire job
The stored data file size keeps growing over time
The display palette colors slowly shift about on screen
content.explanation: Conditions and equipment can drift, so periodic checks (and at the end of a scan set) confirm the setup is still valid, with re-scans if it has shifted.
distractors: The response can change, so rechecks are needed.
Growing file size does not require recalibration.
Display palette colors do not drive recalibration.

content.stem: If a periodic check shows the setup has drifted out of tolerance, the technician should:
options: Recalibrate and re-scan the affected data
Accept the drifted data just as it stands
Quietly hide the drift out of the report
Throw the reference block out for good now
content.explanation: Out-of-tolerance drift can invalidate data taken since the last good check, so the setup is corrected and the affected area re-scanned.
distractors: Drifted data is not simply accepted.
Drift is reported and corrected, not hidden.
The reference block is kept, not deleted.

content.stem: A common reference reflector for phased array sensitivity and TCG is the:
options: Side-drilled hole
A painted ink dot
Couplant droplet
The coiled cable
content.explanation: Side-drilled holes give consistent, repeatable reflections at known depths, widely used for TCG and sensitivity. Confirm the required reflector against the procedure.
distractors: A painted dot is not an ultrasonic reference reflector.
A couplant droplet is not a reference reflector.
A cable loop is not a reference reflector.

content.stem: A machined radius on a calibration block is useful for setting the:
options: Wedge delay and verifying angles
Just the couplant viscosity in use
Just the display screen brightness
Just the plain probe scan speed
content.explanation: The radius returns a strong echo from a known geometry, helping set the wedge delay (zero) and confirm the refracted angles.
distractors: Couplant viscosity is not set by the radius.
Display brightness is not set from the radius.
Scan speed is not set from the radius.

content.stem: The calibration should be:
options: Recorded with the block, reflectors, and settings used
Kept only in the unit's volatile memory and nowhere else
Thrown straight out right after the work is done with it
Picked out at random rather than from the set procedure
content.explanation: Documenting the calibration (block, reflectors, velocity, delay, gains, gates) supports repeatability and traceability.
distractors: Memory is not a reliable calibration record.
Calibration records are retained, not discarded.
Calibration follows the procedure, not random choices.

content.stem: Scanning gain is set relative to the:
options: Calibrated reference level, per the procedure
The very loudest signal that happens to turn up
The first stray echo that happens to be seen
The chosen display color palette on the screen
content.explanation: Scanning sensitivity is referenced to the calibrated reflector level (often with an added scan gain per the procedure), keeping it consistent and traceable.
distractors: Gain is referenced to a known level, not simply the loudest signal.
Gain is referenced to a calibrated level, not the first echo seen.
The display palette does not set the scanning gain.

content.stem: The calibration block material should be:
options: Acoustically similar to the part being inspected
Any unrelated metal grabbed straight off the bench
Always a soft lead block, whatever the test part
Always a plastic block, whatever the test part is
content.explanation: A block with similar velocity and attenuation makes the calibration represent the part; an unrelated material would not.
distractors: An unrelated metal may not represent the part acoustically.
Lead is not a representative test block material here.
Plastic does not represent a metal part acoustically.

content.stem: Verifying that each focal law performs as intended is part of:
options: Setup verification before scanning
Final acceptance evaluation of it
The probe array manufacturing work
Writing the governing site code now
content.explanation: Confirming angles, depth, and sensitivity for the focal laws is a setup-verification step done before acquiring data, within the Level I scope under direction.
distractors: Final acceptance is a Level II task, separate from setup verification.
Probe manufacturing is not the technician's verification step.
Code writing is a higher-level activity.

content.stem: Instead of TCG, some procedures use a distance-amplitude correction (DAC) curve to:
options: Reference amplitude versus sound path
Steer the beam round to each new angle
Drive power into the entire probe array
Set the encoder counts along the scan
content.explanation: A DAC curve plots the reference reflector amplitude against distance, against which signals are compared, an alternative to flattening with TCG. Follow the procedure.
distractors: Steering is done by the focal laws, not a DAC curve.
A DAC curve does not power the probe.
A DAC curve does not define encoder counts.

content.stem: Coupling during calibration should represent scanning because poor coupling would:
options: Give a false reference level
Sharply improve the accuracy
Tighten up the beam focus
Speed up the data acquisition
content.explanation: If the reference is set with poor coupling, the sensitivity will be wrong during scanning, so consistent coupling is maintained.
distractors: Poor coupling harms, not improves, accuracy.
Poor coupling lowers signal; it does not tighten the focus.
Poor coupling does not speed up acquisition.

content.stem: Velocity and wedge delay are calibrated so that a known reflector appears at its:
options: Correct depth and position
Peak maximum amplitude only
Some plain random location
Plain zero on every axis
content.explanation: Correct velocity and delay place known reflectors at their true depth and position, confirming the geometry of the setup.
distractors: Amplitude is a separate sensitivity step, not the position calibration.
Known reflectors should appear at known, not random, locations.
They appear at their true location, not zero everywhere.

content.stem: Encoder setup also confirms the scan records in the:
options: Correct direction and distance
The wrong way round to save time
Just the highest gain level set
Just the brightest color palette
content.explanation: Checking direction and distance ensures images are not reversed or mis-scaled, so reflectors map to the right place on the part.
distractors: Recording in the wrong direction would misplace data.
Gain is unrelated to encoder direction and distance.
The display palette is unrelated to encoder direction and distance.

content.stem: Reference reflectors are used because they:
options: Give known, repeatable responses to set the setup
Are the actual service flaws that are being sought
Speed the sound up sharply as it passes by each one
Soak up the entire beam so that none of it returns
content.explanation: Known reflectors provide consistent echoes to calibrate velocity, delay, gain, and sensitivity, unlike unknown real flaws.
distractors: Reference reflectors are deliberate known shapes, not the actual flaws.
They reflect sound at a known shape; they do not speed it up.
They reflect sound rather than absorbing it all.

content.stem: Many procedures require a calibration check:
options: At the start and again at the end of a scan set
Just one single time across each full year only
Never once at any single point at all over it
Only when a brand-new probe array gets fitted
content.explanation: Checking at the start and end (and at intervals) confirms the setup held throughout, so data taken between valid checks can be accepted. Confirm intervals against the procedure.
distractors: Checks are per scan set or interval, not annual.
Checks are required, not skipped.
Checks apply regardless of probe age.

content.stem: The reference and scan gains should be set so the instrument:
options: Has usable range without saturating signals of interest
Is always run flat out at the very maximum gain setting
Is run right down at a dead zero gain level throughout
Pays the calibrated reference level no real mind at all
content.explanation: Appropriate gain keeps relevant signals on scale and measurable rather than saturated or buried, referenced to the calibration.
distractors: Always running at maximum can saturate and clip signals.
Zero gain would hide signals.
The reference is used, not ignored.

content.stem: In calibration and verification, the Level I technician:
options: Performs and records the calibration per the procedure under direction
Sets the entire accept and reject criteria for the welded joint alone
Designs the reference calibration block and its reflectors for the job
Writes and approves the entire inspection procedure for the site to use
content.explanation: A Level I calibrates and verifies the setup and records it per the procedure; criteria, block design, and procedure approval are higher-level functions.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Designing the reference block is not a Level I task.
Approving the procedure is above the Level I.

content.stem: Verifying the setup on a reference block before scanning is important because:
options: Wrong inputs or wear could mislocate or miss reflectors
It just wastes good scanning time for no real gain at all
The probe quietly self-corrects every setup error by itself
Fresh couplant gel fixes every setup error there is
content.explanation: Setup errors and equipment wear can mislocate reflectors or lose sensitivity, so verification catches them before real data is taken.
distractors: Verification prevents costly errors; it is not wasted time.
The probe does not self-correct setup errors.
Couplant does not fix setup or calibration errors.

content.stem: If dead elements are found, the technician should:
options: Address the probe before relying on the calibration
Calibrate and scan straight on with it regardless
Wind the gain right up to cover over the dead gap
Just ignore it entirely and carry on with the work
content.explanation: Dead elements distort the beam and invalidate the calibration, so the probe is repaired or replaced before proceeding.
distractors: Calibrating and scanning with dead elements gives invalid data.
Adding gain does not fix a distorted beam.
Dead elements affect results and are not ignored.

content.stem: A large temperature change between calibration and scanning can:
options: Shift velocity and wedge delay, requiring recalibration
Have no real effect on the entire setup at any point
Change the accept and reject criteria for the entire job
Add fresh elements onto the probe array by itself
content.explanation: Temperature alters material and wedge velocities and coupling, shifting readings, so the setup is rechecked or recalibrated when conditions change.
distractors: Temperature does affect the setup.
Temperature does not change the acceptance criteria.
Temperature does not add elements to the probe.

content.stem: Which statement about calibration and verification is correct?
options: Set velocity and wedge delay, build TCG/ACG and reference sensitivity, calibrate the encoder, and verify on a reference block before and during scanning
Calibration is entirely optional for phased array work, since the instrument sets its own velocity, wedge delay, and sensitivity by itself every time
Running flat out at maximum gain fully replaces the need to calibrate, so velocity, wedge delay, and reference sensitivity never have to be set at all
Dead elements in the probe have no real effect on the calibration or the beam at all, so a probe with several dead elements can be calibrated and used just as it is
content.explanation: Phased array calibration sets the geometry and sensitivity, corrects gain across depth and angle, calibrates position, and is verified on reference reflectors before and during the work.
distractors: Calibration is required, not optional.
Maximum gain does not replace calibration.
Dead elements distort the beam and do affect calibration.

content.stem: A common phased array weld technique is an encoded line scan, where the probe is:
options: Moved along the weld at a fixed offset while position is recorded
Held dead still over the entire weld for the full scanning time
Lifted clean off the surface between each of the readings taken
Pressed down a good deal harder at each end of the weld run
content.explanation: The probe runs parallel to the weld at a set offset while the encoder records position, capturing a continuous data record of the weld length.
distractors: Holding still would not cover the weld length.
Lifting the probe loses coupling and data.
Encoded scanning moves the probe at a steady offset, not by pressing at the ends.

content.stem: The probe offset from the weld centerline is set so that the:
options: Beams cover the weld volume per the scan plan
Probe sits right up on top of the weld cap
The probe cable stays nice and short on the run
The couplant looks nice and even on the surface
content.explanation: The standoff (index offset) places the angled beams to cover the weld from root to cap as the scan plan requires.
distractors: The probe is offset to angle into the weld, not sit on the cap.
Cable length does not set the offset.
Couplant appearance does not set the offset.

content.stem: A raster scan differs from a single-line scan because it:
options: Covers multiple index lines across the area
Uses no position encoder at all on the rig
Needs no couplant on the surface at all
Skips the entire calibration step each time
content.explanation: A raster steps the probe across several index positions to cover a wider area, while a single-line scan runs one offset along the weld.
distractors: Raster scanning still uses an encoder.
Couplant is still required.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: Scanning too fast can cause:
options: Missed scan lines or data gaps
Far sharper image resolution
A higher material velocity
A brand-new focal law set
content.explanation: If the probe outruns the data rate (set by PRF and number of laws), lines are skipped, so scan speed is kept within the limit for full data.
distractors: Excess speed loses data; it does not improve resolution.
Speed does not change material velocity.
Speed does not create a focal law.

content.stem: A steady couplant supply during scanning helps prevent:
options: Coupling loss and data dropout
A correct calibration setup
The encoder tracking it well
The focal-law set being formed
content.explanation: Consistent couplant keeps the beam entering the part as the probe moves, avoiding gaps in the data.
distractors: Couplant supply supports, not prevents, correct calibration.
Couplant does not stop encoder tracking.
Couplant does not generate focal laws.

content.stem: Welds are often scanned from both sides because:
options: Different flaw orientations are better detected from each side
One single side is always plenty enough by itself for any weld
It gets through a fair bit less couplant gel over the entire job
It keeps the probe cable run back to the unit a good deal shorter
content.explanation: Scanning both sides improves the chance of intersecting flaws of various orientations and covering the full weld volume, per the scan plan.
distractors: One side may miss flaws favorable to the other side.
Two-sided scanning is about coverage, not couplant savings.
It does not change the cable.

content.stem: An S-scan helps cover a weld because its angles can reach:
options: From the root to the cap region of the weld
Only the outer surface of the weld itself
Only the zone sitting outside the part
Only along the length of the probe cable run
content.explanation: The swept angles, combined with the probe offset and skip, let the beams cover the weld from root to cap as planned.
distractors: The angles cover the volume, not only the surface.
The beams cover the weld, not outside the part.
Coverage concerns the weld, not the cable.

content.stem: Using first-leg and second-leg (skip) paths lets the beam:
options: Reach different depths of the weld via reflection off the far surface
Steer clean around the entire weld body and miss it each time
Get away without doing any calibration at all before the scan begins
Stand in for the position encoder on the entire scanning rig
content.explanation: As in conventional angle-beam UT, the half-skip and full-skip legs reach different parts of the weld, extending coverage from a given offset.
distractors: The skip paths cover, not avoid, the weld.
Skip paths do not skip calibration.
Skip paths do not replace the encoder.

content.stem: Maintaining a consistent probe offset during scanning is important because it:
options: Keeps the planned coverage and position accuracy
Cools the entire probe array right down on the job
Changes the material velocity used in the part
Builds the entire image data set up by itself
content.explanation: A guide or scanner holds the offset so the beams stay on the planned coverage and reflector positions are computed correctly.
distractors: Consistent offset is about coverage, not cooling.
Offset does not change material velocity.
Offset does not develop data.

content.stem: Probe skew (misalignment to the weld axis) can:
options: Distort coverage and reflector positions
Sharpen up the coverage across the weld
Raise the probe operating frequency set
Stand in for the entire written scan plan
content.explanation: If the probe is not aligned to the scan axis, the beams and recorded positions are off, so alignment is controlled with guides or a scanner.
distractors: Skew degrades, not improves, coverage.
Skew does not change frequency.
Skew does not replace the scan plan.

content.stem: The scan resolution (data spacing along the scan) is set by the:
options: Encoder step and acquisition rate
The plain couplant gel type used
The chosen display color palette
The set receiver gain level value
content.explanation: How finely data is sampled along the scan depends on the encoder resolution and the acquisition rate, balanced against scan speed.
distractors: Couplant type does not set scan resolution.
The display palette does not set scan resolution.
Gain does not set scan resolution.

content.stem: Before scanning, the surface is prepared so that:
options: The probe couples consistently and moves smoothly
The couplant gel changes its color on the surface
The probe cable run comes out a fair bit shorter
The probe operating frequency climbs up as it goes
content.explanation: Removing spatter, scale, and roughness lets the probe maintain coupling and a steady offset, improving data quality.
distractors: Surface prep is about coupling, not couplant color.
Surface prep does not change the cable.
Surface prep does not change the frequency.

content.stem: During or after scanning, the technician checks that the data shows:
options: The planned coverage with no missed areas
Only the prettiest-looking image on screen
The fewest possible saved data files
The very lowest receiver gain setting
content.explanation: Coverage is verified against the scan plan, looking for gaps or dropout, with re-scans where coverage was not achieved.
distractors: A pretty image does not prove coverage.
The fewest files is not the goal; complete coverage is.
Low gain is not the coverage check.

content.stem: If coupling is lost over part of a scan, the technician should:
options: Re-scan the affected area
Just accept the gap as is
Drop the gain to mask it
Delete the entire data file
content.explanation: A coupling gap leaves the area unexamined, so it is re-scanned to obtain valid data over the full length.
distractors: A coverage gap is not simply accepted.
Lowering gain does not recover missed data.
The file is kept and the area re-scanned, not deleted.

content.stem: On small-diameter pipe, the probe and wedge must:
options: Fit the curvature for proper contact and angles
Be the very largest pair available on the rig
Pay the pipe curvature no real mind at all on it
Be run fully dry with no couplant at all on them
content.explanation: A curved surface needs a matching (contoured) wedge so the probe couples and the angles stay correct around the pipe.
distractors: The largest probe may not fit the curvature.
Curvature must be accounted for, not ignored.
Coupling still requires couplant, not a dry run.

content.stem: The angles, offsets, and coverage used during scanning come from the:
options: Scan plan and procedure
The operator's own whim
The couplant tin label
The probe cable diagram
content.explanation: A Level I follows the scan plan and procedure, which define the focal laws, offsets, and coverage for the inspection.
distractors: Scanning follows the plan, not personal preference.
The couplant label does not define coverage.
A cable diagram does not define coverage.

content.stem: In a raster scan, adjacent index lines should:
options: Overlap enough to leave no gaps
Leave wide gaps just to save time
Never quite touch one another
Be spaced right out at random
content.explanation: Overlapping index passes ensure the area is fully covered with no unexamined strips between lines.
distractors: Wide gaps would leave areas unexamined.
Lines must cover the area, not avoid touching.
Index spacing follows the plan, not random choice.

content.stem: The maximum scan speed for full data depends partly on the:
options: Pulse repetition frequency and number of focal laws
The couplant gel type chosen for the scan job
The display color palette set on the entire screen
The overall length of the final written job report
content.explanation: More focal laws per position and a limited PRF reduce how fast the probe can move before lines are missed, so speed is matched to the setup.
distractors: Couplant type does not set the speed limit.
The display palette does not set the speed limit.
Report length does not set the speed limit.

content.stem: Consistent probe contact and pressure during scanning help:
options: Maintain coupling and steady signals
Change the accept and reject criteria
Steer the beam round to new angles
Generate the entire focal-law set
content.explanation: Even contact keeps the sound entering the part consistently, avoiding amplitude swings and dropout as the probe moves.
distractors: Contact does not change acceptance criteria.
Steering comes from the focal laws, not probe pressure.
Focal laws are generated in software, not by probe pressure.

content.stem: Scanning should extend far enough past the weld ends to:
options: Cover the full required length including the ends
Stop well short of the weld ends just to save time
Cover only the middle stretch of the weld run
Steer well clear of the entire heat-affected zone
content.explanation: Running the scan past the ends ensures the whole required length, including weld ends, is covered with the encoded data.
distractors: Stopping short leaves ends unexamined.
Covering only the middle misses the ends.
The heat-affected zone is part of what is examined, not avoided.

content.stem: Some setups use multiple probe groups so that:
options: Different angles or zones are covered together
No calibration is needed at all for the job
The entire position encoder is dropped off fully
The couplant gel can be skipped entirely on it
content.explanation: Multiple groups (or probes) can acquire complementary coverage in one pass, configured in the setup and still calibrated and coupled.
distractors: Multiple groups still require calibration.
An encoder is still used for position.
Couplant is still required.

content.stem: A finer encoder step during scanning gives:
options: More data points per length (finer sampling)
Coarser sampling along the entire scan line
Fewer focal laws in the entire set being used
A lower probe operating frequency on the job
content.explanation: Smaller steps sample the scan more finely, improving along-scan resolution at the cost of data volume and possibly slower scanning.
distractors: A finer step gives finer, not coarser, sampling.
Encoder step does not set the number of focal laws.
Encoder step does not change the frequency.

content.stem: If the scan plan requires it, the weld cap may be:
options: Dressed so the probe can reach the needed offset
Left fully rough each time with no dressing at all
Built up higher with extra added weld metal first
Notched deeply across the cap at each end first
content.explanation: Where access or coverage requires, the cap is dressed flush so the probe can sit at the planned offset, per the procedure.
distractors: A rough cap can block the needed probe position.
Adding weld metal blocks access; the cap is dressed down, not up.
Notching the cap damages the weld; it is not access prep.

content.stem: Encoded scanning is preferred for documented inspections because it:
options: Produces a position-tied record that can be reviewed
Cannot be saved off to a file at all afterward later
Does away with the need for any scan coverage at all
Gets rid of the entire calibration step on it
content.explanation: Position-encoded data forms a reviewable, traceable record of what was covered, unlike a live-only display.
distractors: Encoded data is saved, not unsavable.
Coverage is still required and is verified from the data.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: If the encoder slips or loses tracking during a scan, the data may be:
options: Mispositioned, so the scan is repeated
Perfectly fine just the way it stands
Put right by itself without any help
Far more accurate than it was before
content.explanation: Encoder slip misplaces the data along the part, so the affected scan is repeated with the tracking restored.
distractors: Slipped tracking misplaces data; it is not fine.
Slip is not automatically corrected.
Slip degrades, not improves, accuracy.

content.stem: Removing loose scale or debris ahead of the probe during scanning helps:
options: Keep coupling and a smooth, steady scan
Change the entire focal-law set in use
Raise the probe operating frequency set
Set the accept and reject criteria
content.explanation: Debris under the probe causes lift-off and dropout, so the scan path is kept clean for consistent data.
distractors: Cleaning does not change the focal laws.
Cleaning does not raise the frequency.
Cleaning does not set acceptance criteria.

content.stem: Coverage and probe positions should follow the scan plan rather than:
options: Memory of a different joint
The written work procedure
The calibrated setup in use
The encoder position readout
content.explanation: Each joint is scanned to its own plan; relying on a different job's memory can leave the required coverage unmet.
distractors: The written procedure is a correct source, not something to avoid.
The calibrated setup is used as intended.
The encoder reading is used for position.

content.stem: If surface temperature changes a lot during a long scan, the technician should:
options: Recheck the calibration and conditions
Just ignore it entirely and press on
Wind the gain up blindly to cope with it
Delete the entire gathered data set
content.explanation: Temperature shifts can change velocity and coupling, so the setup is rechecked and the data confirmed valid, with re-scans if needed.
distractors: Temperature change is not ignored.
Blindly raising gain does not address a calibration shift.
Data is reviewed, not deleted.

content.stem: When several passes are needed, overlapping them ensures:
options: The whole required volume is examined
Only the easy spots get covered well
The entire probe array wears down evenly
The probe cable run stays nice and cool
content.explanation: Overlapping passes prevent unexamined gaps between them, giving complete coverage of the required volume.
distractors: Overlap is for full coverage, not just easy areas.
Overlap is about coverage, not probe wear.
Overlap is about coverage, not cable temperature.

content.stem: While scanning, the Level I technician:
options: Executes the scan plan and acquires valid data under direction
Sets the entire accept and reject criteria for the welded joint
Designs the entire scan plan for the inspection job alone
Approves the entire results against the governing code alone
content.explanation: A Level I runs the scan plan, maintains coupling and coverage, and acquires data; designing the plan, setting criteria, and code approval are higher-level tasks.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Designing the scan plan is above the Level I.
Approving results to code is a higher-level task.

content.stem: Before leaving the job, the technician confirms there are:
options: No missed lines or uncovered length in the data
Just a few small coverage gaps left in it
As few saved data files as can be managed
The very shortest overall scan time of all
content.explanation: The data is reviewed for completeness so any missed lines or uncovered areas are re-scanned before the inspection is considered done.
distractors: Gaps mean areas were not examined and must be re-scanned.
Minimizing files is not the goal; complete coverage is.
Shortest time is not the goal; complete data is.

content.stem: Using the correct wedge for the surface keeps the:
options: Refracted angles and coupling as intended
The scan speed pinned up at its maximum
The receiver gain held right down at zero
The saved data file size kept small
content.explanation: A wedge matched to the surface and material keeps the planned angles and good contact, so coverage and positions stay correct.
distractors: The wedge sets angles and coupling; it does not maximize scan speed.
The wedge does not set the gain to zero.
The wedge does not control file size.

content.stem: Scan parameters such as offset, speed limits, and couplant should be:
options: Followed per the plan and noted in the record
Picked out at random by whoever is on the day
Kept hidden away from any later review at all
Left fully out of the written record entirely
content.explanation: Following and recording the scan conditions supports repeatability and lets reviewers confirm the inspection was done as planned.
distractors: Parameters follow the plan, not random choice.
Parameters are documented, not hidden.
Conditions are recorded, not left out.

content.stem: Which statement about scanning and coverage is correct?
options: Run encoded scans at the planned offset and speed, keep coupling, cover the full volume from the required sides, and verify no gaps
Run the scan as fast as the probe will go, whatever happens to the data, since speed matters far more than catching every line
Scanning one single side in one single pass is always plenty for any weld, with no need for the other side or any overlapping passes
Coverage gaps are fine and can be left in the data to save time, since a clean-looking image proves the full volume was examined
content.explanation: Phased array scanning follows the plan for offset, angles, and speed, maintains coupling, covers the volume from the required sides, and is verified for complete data.
distractors: Excess speed loses data and is not acceptable.
Coverage often needs both sides and overlapping passes.
Coverage gaps leave the part unexamined and are re-scanned.

content.stem: Acquired encoded data should be:
options: Saved as identified files tied to the part and scan
Deleted right off after one single quick look at it
Kept only up on the live screen view and nowhere else
Left fully unnamed and unlabelled in the file store
content.explanation: The data files, with identification and position, are saved as the inspection record for review and traceability.
distractors: Data is retained, not deleted after viewing.
Data is saved to file, not kept only on screen.
Files are identified, not left unnamed.

content.stem: Good acquisition data shows adequate sensitivity, full coverage, and:
options: Acceptable signal-to-noise without dropout
The most noise possible across the entire trace
Random gaps dotted along the entire scan line
Saturated signals right across the display
content.explanation: Quality data has the reference sensitivity, complete coverage, low dropout, and adequate signal-to-noise so reflectors can be reviewed.
distractors: High noise degrades, not helps, the data.
Random gaps mean missed coverage.
Saturation clips signals and hides detail.

content.stem: Reviewing the data for missed lines or gaps is done to:
options: Confirm coverage before leaving the job
Set the accept and reject criteria used
Recompute the entire focal-law set anew
Reset the encoder zero point all over
content.explanation: Checking for dropout and missed scan lines confirms the required coverage was achieved, with re-scans where it was not.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not this quality check.
Reviewing for gaps does not recalculate the focal laws.
Reviewing for gaps does not reset the encoder.

content.stem: Sudden low-amplitude or blank regions in the data often indicate:
options: Coupling loss or lift-off during the scan
A perfectly clean scan the entire way through
A higher material velocity reading shown
A brand-new acceptance limit set for it
content.explanation: Dropout usually means the probe lost coupling or lifted off, so the cause is corrected and the area re-scanned.
distractors: Dropout indicates a problem, not a perfect scan.
Dropout is not a velocity change.
Dropout is not an acceptance limit.

content.stem: Signals of interest should generally not be:
options: Saturated (clipped at full scale)
Plainly visible up on the display
Held neatly within the set gates
Referenced back to the calibration
content.explanation: Saturated signals lose amplitude information, so gain is set to keep relevant signals on scale for valid measurement and review.
distractors: Signals of interest should be visible, which is intended.
Signals should be within the gates, which is intended.
Referencing to calibration is correct, not something to avoid.

content.stem: A low signal-to-noise ratio in the data can:
options: Make real reflectors hard to distinguish from noise
Improve the detectability of every small flaw
Raise the probe operating frequency right up on it
Shorten the probe cable run back to the entire unit
content.explanation: When noise approaches signal levels, reflectors are harder to see, so probe choice, gain, and setup aim for adequate signal-to-noise.
distractors: Low signal-to-noise harms, not improves, detectability.
Signal-to-noise is not the frequency.
Signal-to-noise is unrelated to cable length.

content.stem: Each data file should carry identification that ties it to the:
options: Part, weld, and scan details
The set display palette in use
Just the gain value by itself
Just the scan speed by itself
content.explanation: Identification (part, weld, location, date, technician, setup) makes the data traceable and reviewable.
distractors: The display palette is not the file identification.
The gain value alone is not file identification.
Scan speed alone is not file identification.

content.stem: The calibration or setup used should be:
options: Saved or referenced with the scan data
Thrown out right after all the scanning
Kept secret away from any later review
Randomized afresh for each single file
content.explanation: Storing the setup and calibration with the data lets reviewers confirm the data was taken with a valid, known configuration.
distractors: The calibration is retained, not discarded.
It is documented, not kept secret.
The setup is consistent, not randomized.

content.stem: Gates during acquisition are used to:
options: Measure and record signals in the regions of interest
Steer the beam round to one single chosen angle
Build the entire cross-section image by themselves
Drive the power out to the position encoder on the rig
content.explanation: Gates capture amplitude and position data in the time or depth zones of interest, feeding the imaging and measurements.
distractors: Steering comes from the focal law; gates select a signal window.
The image views are built from A-scans; gates select windows.
Gates do not power the encoder.

content.stem: Important scan data should be:
options: Backed up to prevent loss
Stored on one device only
Wiped to free up space
Held in volatile memory
content.explanation: Backing up the data protects the inspection record against device failure or accidental loss.
distractors: A single copy risks loss.
Records are retained, not deleted for space.
Volatile memory alone risks losing the data.

content.stem: Reviewing data on-site for quality is done so that:
options: Re-scans can be made while still set up
The Level I makes the final accept call
The entire set procedure can be skipped
The position encoder can be dropped off
content.explanation: Checking quality before leaving lets the technician re-scan poor areas immediately. Final acceptance remains a higher-level task.
distractors: On-site quality review is not the final acceptance decision.
The procedure is still followed.
The encoder is still needed for position.

content.stem: The recorded amplitudes are meaningful only if the:
options: Reference sensitivity was correctly set and maintained
The scan was run at the very fastest speed of all
The palette was flipped to the full rainbow set in use
The saved data file came out the very smallest of all
content.explanation: Amplitudes are read relative to the calibrated reference, so a correct, maintained reference is essential for the data to mean anything.
distractors: Scan speed does not validate amplitudes; the reference does.
The palette choice does not validate amplitudes.
File size does not validate amplitudes.

content.stem: If the data positions do not match the part length, the likely cause is:
options: An encoder calibration or tracking problem
A perfectly correct setup all round on it
A higher probe operating frequency in use
A fresh batch of couplant gel on the surface
content.explanation: Position errors point to encoder calibration or slip, so the encoder is checked and the scan repeated with correct tracking.
distractors: A correct setup would give matching positions.
Frequency does not cause position mismatch.
Couplant freshness does not cause position mismatch.

content.stem: An indication that may be a grating lobe or geometry signal should be:
options: Recognized as a possible artifact, with evaluation left to a higher level
Logged straight off as a confirmed rejectable flaw right there on the spot
Wiped clean out of the recorded data set straight away there and then
Passed over entirely and left clean out of the report and the data both
content.explanation: The technician notes that not all indications are flaws and preserves the data; confirming and evaluating is a higher-level task.
distractors: It is not confirmed as a flaw by the Level I.
Data is preserved, not erased.
Indications are recorded, not ignored.

content.stem: Electrical noise in the data can come from:
options: Poor grounding, cables, or nearby equipment
A perfectly correct calibration setup on it
Good steady coupling right on the surface
A nice clean, smooth scanning surface on it
content.explanation: Noise sources include grounding and cable issues and interference, which are reduced so signals stand out clearly.
distractors: Correct calibration does not add noise.
Good coupling reduces, not adds, dropout and noise.
A clean surface helps, not hurts, the data.

content.stem: The scan and display resolution must be adequate to:
options: Show the reflectors the inspection is meant to find
Fill up the storage disk the very fastest of all
Use up the most display colors of all on the screen
Run the entire probe array the very hottest of all
content.explanation: Resolution is set so relevant reflectors are sampled and visible; too coarse a setting can miss small or closely spaced indications.
distractors: Filling the disk is not the goal of resolution.
Color count is not the goal of resolution.
Probe temperature is unrelated to resolution.

content.stem: When acquired data is poor quality, the technician should:
options: Correct the cause and re-scan
Just submit it as it is anyway
Touch it up so it looks better
Wipe the evidence clean off it
content.explanation: Poor data is not valid, so the cause (coupling, speed, setup) is fixed and the area re-scanned rather than submitted or altered.
distractors: Submitting poor data risks missing flaws.
Altering data is falsification.
Deleting data destroys the record.

content.stem: Amplitude variations along a scan that follow coupling changes indicate the need to:
options: Improve and steady the coupling
Raise the entire acceptance limit
Change the probe frequency set
Shorten the entire probe cable run
content.explanation: Coupling-related amplitude swings reduce reliability, so coupling is improved and the area re-scanned for consistent data.
distractors: Acceptance limits are not changed to mask coupling issues.
Frequency is not the fix for coupling variation.
Cable length is not the fix for coupling variation.

content.stem: Acquiring and checking the data for quality is a Level I task, while interpreting and sizing reflectors is:
options: A Level II or III task
Also just a Level I task
Done by the encoder unit
Set by the couplant gel
content.explanation: A Level I produces valid, complete data; analysis, sizing, and evaluation against criteria are higher-level responsibilities.
distractors: Interpretation and sizing are above the Level I.
The encoder records position; it does not interpret.
The couplant does not interpret the data.

content.stem: The gain, reference level, and gate settings used are:
options: Recorded with the data
Lost track of afterward
Kept hidden from view
Just set at random
content.explanation: Recording the acquisition settings lets the data be understood, reproduced, and reviewed.
distractors: Settings are recorded, not forgotten.
Settings are documented, not secret.
Settings follow the setup, not randomization.

content.stem: Before finishing, the technician confirms that the data shows the:
options: Scan plan was actually executed as required
The fastest possible scan time was hit on it
The fewest possible data files were saved
The brightest screen colors were used on it
content.explanation: Confirming the angles, coverage, and offsets in the data match the scan plan ensures the inspection was carried out as required.
distractors: Speed is not the confirmation of plan execution.
File count is not the confirmation.
Color brightness is not the confirmation.

content.stem: If reference or relevant signals are saturating, the technician should:
options: Adjust gain so they are measurable and re-acquire
Just leave them clipped at full scale as they are
Wind the gain up even further still over the top
Just ignore it fully and press straight on with it
content.explanation: Clipped signals cannot be measured, so gain is set to bring them on scale and the affected data is re-acquired.
distractors: Leaving signals clipped loses information.
More gain worsens saturation.
Saturation is corrected, not ignored.

content.stem: A consistent file-naming and identification scheme helps:
options: Trace each scan to the correct weld and location
Hide which weld it was that got actually scanned
Cut down on the entire probe array wear over time
Drop the probe operating frequency down on it
content.explanation: Clear naming ties data to the right joint and location, supporting review and traceability.
distractors: Naming is for traceability, not hiding.
Naming does not affect probe wear.
Naming does not change the frequency.

content.stem: The acquired data must never be:
options: Altered to change the apparent result
Saved with its full identification
Backed up safely to a second store
Reviewed closely for overall quality
content.explanation: Falsifying or altering data to change results is a serious violation; the data is preserved, identified, and reviewed honestly.
distractors: Saving with identification is correct practice.
Backing up is correct practice.
Reviewing for quality is correct practice.

content.stem: If review shows an area was not covered, the technician should:
options: Re-scan that area to complete coverage
Report full coverage anyway all the same
Average straight over the entire gap area
Delete the surrounding data all round it
content.explanation: An uncovered area is examined by re-scanning, since reporting full coverage without it would be false.
distractors: Reporting coverage that was not achieved is false.
Averaging does not examine the missed area.
Deleting data does not fix a coverage gap.

content.stem: Significant conditions during acquisition, such as temperature, should be:
options: Noted with the data when relevant
Always left clean off entirely
Hidden away from any later review
Set down at random every time
content.explanation: Recording relevant conditions helps reviewers judge the data and supports traceability.
distractors: Relevant conditions are noted, not omitted.
Conditions are documented, not hidden.
Conditions are recorded accurately, not randomized.

content.stem: The best time to catch a coverage or quality problem is:
options: On-site, while still set up to re-scan
After every hand has left the entire site
At no single point during the job
Only back at the home office later on
content.explanation: Reviewing data quality on-site allows immediate re-scans, avoiding a return trip and an incomplete record.
distractors: After leaving, re-scanning requires returning.
Quality problems should be caught, not never.
Catching it only at the office is too late to re-scan easily.

content.stem: If an end-of-scan calibration check fails, the data since the last good check is:
options: Suspect and the affected area is re-scanned
Taken as valid by itself automatically
Taken as far better off than it was before
Wiped for good clean off the storage unit
content.explanation: A failed check casts doubt on data taken since the last valid check, so that area is recalibrated and re-scanned.
distractors: A failed check makes data suspect, not automatically valid.
A failed check does not improve data.
Data is reviewed and re-scanned, not permanently deleted.

content.stem: In data acquisition, the Level I technician:
options: Acquires, checks quality, and records data under direction
Carries out the entire final evaluation of the joint alone
Writes the entire accept and reject criteria for the job
Certifies the entire inspection procedure for site use
content.explanation: A Level I acquires valid, complete, identified data and checks its quality; evaluation, criteria, and procedure approval are higher-level functions.
distractors: Final evaluation is a Level II task.
Writing acceptance criteria is above the Level I.
Certifying the procedure is above the Level I.

content.stem: Which statement about data acquisition and quality is correct?
options: Acquire complete, identified, well-coupled data at the reference sensitivity, check it for coverage and quality, and re-scan poor areas
Saturated, noisy data is perfectly fine just as it stands, since clipped signals and heavy grass have no bearing on whether a flaw is found
The recorded data may be freely altered afterward to make the part pass, as long as the final image still looks tidy on screen
Coverage gaps in the recorded data need no action at all and can be left as they are, since the rest of the scan went perfectly fine
content.explanation: Quality phased array data is complete, identified, properly coupled and referenced, and free of saturation and dropout, with poor areas re-scanned and nothing altered.
distractors: Saturated, noisy data is not acceptable.
Altering data is falsification.
Coverage gaps are re-scanned, not ignored.

content.stem: Compared with radiography, phased array ultrasonic testing presents:
options: No ionizing-radiation hazard from the method itself
A serious ionizing-radiation exposure hazard to nearby workers
A need to license the radioactive source it carries
A need for a fully shielded enclosure round it all
content.explanation: Phased array uses sound, so the method itself has no ionizing-radiation hazard, though general industrial hazards still apply.
distractors: Phased array does not emit ionizing radiation.
No radioactive source is used, so no source license is needed.
Shielded enclosures are for radiation work; phased array emits sound.

content.stem: General safety hazards during phased array work include:
options: Electrical, mechanical, access, and confined-space risks
Ionizing radiation given off straight by the probe array
Radioactive decay coming off the probe array element
Harmful ionizing radiation given off from the probe face
content.explanation: Hazards come from electrical equipment, moving machinery, working at height or in confined spaces, and the work environment, not from the ultrasound.
distractors: The probe emits sound, not ionizing radiation.
No radioactive decay is involved.
No gamma exposure comes from phased array.

content.stem: If radiography is being performed nearby, the phased array technician should:
options: Observe radiation barriers and controls for that other work
Ignore it entirely, since PAUT itself gives off no radiation
Walk freely into the roped-off controlled area anyway
Take down the posted radiation area warning signs nearby
content.explanation: Radiation from a neighboring crew is a real hazard, so the technician respects their barriers, signs, and controls even though PAUT itself has none.
distractors: Another crew's radiation is still a hazard to be respected.
Controlled areas are entered only when safe and permitted.
Safety signage is never removed by an unauthorized person.

content.stem: A Level I technician is qualified to:
options: Set up, calibrate, scan, and record under direction
Interpret and evaluate to the acceptance criteria
Write and approve the entire inspection procedures
Approve the other technicians working on the crew
content.explanation: Level I performs the equipment setup, calibration, scanning, and recording under the direction of higher levels; interpretation and procedure approval are above that scope.
distractors: Interpretation and evaluation are Level II tasks.
Writing and approving procedures is a higher-level function.
Approving personnel is not a Level I role.

content.stem: When unsure whether an indication is a flaw or an artifact, the Level I should:
options: Record it and refer the evaluation to a higher level
Decide the acceptance of it all on their own each time
Erase it clean out of the entire recorded data set
Pass over it entirely and move straight on with it
content.explanation: Evaluation is a higher-level task, so the technician preserves and records the indication and refers the judgment up, rather than deciding or deleting.
distractors: Deciding acceptance is above the Level I scope.
Data is preserved, not erased.
Indications are recorded, not ignored.

content.stem: Altering or fabricating inspection data is:
options: A serious ethical and safety violation
Quite fine when a deadline is very tight
Simply normal everyday working practice
Called for by the governing procedure
content.explanation: Falsifying data can let defective parts pass and endanger people, so it is never acceptable and is a serious violation.
distractors: Deadlines never justify falsifying data.
Falsification is not normal practice.
No procedure requires falsifying data.

content.stem: The technician should perform the inspection:
options: According to the written procedure and scan plan
However happens to look the fastest on the day
From memory of a different past job entirely
With no documentation kept of any of it at all
content.explanation: Following the qualified procedure and scan plan ensures the required coverage, sensitivity, and records are achieved.
distractors: Speed does not override the procedure.
Each job follows its own procedure, not memory of another.
Documentation is part of the procedure.

content.stem: Because phased array is an advanced ultrasonic technique, the technician is expected to understand:
options: Conventional ultrasonic principles it is built on
Only the live free-running view, nothing else
Only the colour palette set on the display
Only the file-naming scheme used on the job
content.explanation: Phased array rests on conventional UT physics, so understanding velocity, refraction, attenuation, and angle-beam work supports correct setup and acquisition.
distractors: A Level I needs the underlying UT principles, not just the live view.
Palette choice is cosmetic; the UT principles underlie the method.
File naming is housekeeping; the UT principles are what underlie it.

content.stem: If the instrument or probe shows a fault during work, the technician should:
options: Stop, report it, and not rely on suspect data
Keep scanning and hope it clears itself soon
Quietly hide the entire fault away from view
Wind the gain right up to mask the fault over
content.explanation: A faulty probe or instrument can invalidate data, so the work stops, the fault is reported and fixed, and affected data is re-checked.
distractors: Scanning with a known fault risks invalid data.
Faults are reported, not hidden.
Adding gain does not fix a hardware fault.

content.stem: Inspection records should let a reviewer:
options: Trace the data to the part, setup, and technician
Guess at which weld it was that ended up scanned
See nothing about the entire setup that was used
Find no real identification on any of it at all
content.explanation: Complete records (part, location, setup, calibration, technician, date) provide traceability and support review.
distractors: Records should remove guessing, not require it.
The setup is part of the record.
Identification is required in the record.

content.stem: A technician should perform only the work for which they are:
options: Qualified and certified
Merely curious about it
Paid the most to do it
Scheduled in earliest
content.explanation: Working within one's qualification and certification protects quality and safety; tasks beyond it are referred to qualified personnel.
distractors: Curiosity does not qualify someone for a task.
Pay does not determine qualification.
Scheduling does not determine qualification.

content.stem: When using mains-powered equipment in the field, the technician should:
options: Check cables and use proper grounding and protection
Pay the frayed power cords no real mind at all on it
Bypass the safety cut-out devices fitted to the gear
Work away in standing water with the gear freely
content.explanation: Electrical safety means inspecting cords, grounding equipment, and using protection, since field conditions can be wet or rugged.
distractors: Frayed cords are a shock hazard and are not ignored.
Safety devices are used, not bypassed.
Working in standing water with electrical gear is hazardous.

content.stem: Before entering a confined space to scan, the technician must:
options: Follow confined-space entry permits and controls
Go straight in right away to save a bit of time
Skip over the atmosphere testing entirely first
Set aside the standing rescue plan for the entry
content.explanation: Confined spaces can hold hazardous atmospheres, so permits, testing, ventilation, and rescue provisions are followed before entry.
distractors: Confined-space entry is never rushed past controls.
Atmosphere testing is required, not skipped.
Rescue provisions are kept in place.

content.stem: Couplant and cleaning materials should be:
options: Handled and disposed of per their safety data and site rules
Just poured out wherever happens to be handy on the day
Taken as always harmless without any check of the safety data
Mixed in with whatever other chemicals happen to be about
content.explanation: Some couplants and cleaners require care, so their safety data sheets and site rules are followed for handling and disposal.
distractors: Couplant is not disposed of carelessly.
Safety data is checked rather than assumed.
Chemicals are not mixed without knowing the hazards.

content.stem: Scanning welds at height requires:
options: Fall protection and safe access per site rules
No special precautions needed on it at all
Taking the guardrails down to get at the work
Free climbing up to reach the weld at height
content.explanation: Elevated work needs proper access, fall protection, and tool security to prevent falls and dropped objects.
distractors: Height work does need precautions.
Guardrails are kept in place.
Free climbing is not safe access.

content.stem: Maintaining data integrity means the records:
options: Truthfully reflect what was scanned and found
Edited about to look that bit cleaner on review
Made to leave inconvenient areas out of it
Copied straight across from some other past job
content.explanation: Honest, complete data that reflects the actual inspection is essential for safe decisions by those who evaluate it.
distractors: Editing to change appearance compromises integrity.
Omitting areas misrepresents coverage.
Copying another job's data is falsification.

content.stem: Interpreting the recorded images, sizing reflectors, and evaluating to the code is the role of a:
options: Level II (or III)
Just the Level I
The probe vendor
A site electrician
content.explanation: Higher levels interpret and evaluate the data the Level I acquires; this division keeps responsibilities clear.
distractors: Interpretation is above the Level I.
The probe vendor supplies hardware, not evaluation.
A site electrician is unrelated to inspection evaluation.

content.stem: Keeping cables, couplant lines, and gear tidy at the work area:
options: Reduces trip and damage hazards
Carries no safety value to it
Helps nothing and slows nothing
Is actively discouraged on site
content.explanation: Good housekeeping prevents trips, dropped equipment, and damage, supporting both safety and data quality.
distractors: Housekeeping does have safety value.
Tidiness reduces hazards and protects gear.
Housekeeping is encouraged, not discouraged.

content.stem: If full coverage could not be achieved due to access, the technician should:
options: Record the limitation honestly
Report full coverage all the same
Hide the limited area clean away
Just guess at what was there
content.explanation: Coverage limitations are documented so reviewers know what was and was not examined, allowing proper decisions.
distractors: Claiming full coverage that was not achieved is false.
Limitations are recorded, not hidden.
Unexamined areas are not guessed at.

content.stem: Required personal protective equipment on site should be:
options: Worn as the site and task require
Skipped when it gets inconvenient
Worn only by the inspectors on site
Optional once working up at height
content.explanation: PPE such as eye, head, hand, and foot protection is worn per site rules and the task hazards.
distractors: PPE is not skipped for convenience.
PPE applies to all who are exposed, not only inspectors.
PPE such as fall protection is required, not optional, at height.

content.stem: Working under direction means the Level I:
options: Carries out the assigned setup and scanning and asks when unsure
Sets the entire inspection requirements for the full job alone
Overrides the entire set procedure at will whenever they please
Works with no oversight at all from any higher level above them
content.explanation: A Level I executes the assigned tasks per the procedure and seeks guidance from higher levels when needed.
distractors: Inspection requirements are set above the Level I.
The procedure is followed, not overridden at will.
A Level I works under the oversight of higher levels.

content.stem: Calibration and setup details are recorded so that:
options: The data can be shown to be valid and repeatable
They can all be safely forgotten about afterward
Nobody is ever able to go back and check them
They stay fully secret away from any later review
content.explanation: Keeping calibration records lets reviewers confirm the data was taken with a valid, traceable setup.
distractors: Records are kept, not forgotten.
Records exist to be checked.
Records support review, not secrecy.

content.stem: Using a motorized scanner or working near rotating equipment, the technician watches for:
options: Pinch points and entanglement hazards
Couplant gel drying out on the wear face
A weak backwall echo on the live screen
Grating lobes in the live S-scan image
content.explanation: Mechanical hazards such as pinch points and entanglement are controlled around scanners and machinery.
distractors: Drying couplant is a coupling issue, not a rotating-equipment hazard.
A weak echo is a signal issue, not a rotating-equipment hazard.
Grating lobes are an imaging artifact, not a mechanical hazard.

content.stem: If the assigned setup does not seem to match the part or procedure, the technician should:
options: Raise the concern before acquiring data
Scan on anyway and keep quiet over it
Alter the procedure quietly on the side
Falsify the scan parameters used for it
content.explanation: Raising a mismatch lets it be corrected before invalid data is taken, which is part of responsible practice under direction.
distractors: Scanning with a wrong setup yields invalid data.
The procedure is not altered secretly.
Parameters are never falsified.

content.stem: Couplant runoff and waste on site should be:
options: Contained and disposed of per site and environmental rules
Just washed off down any handy drain on the entire site
Just left lying about on the open ground wherever it falls
Paid no real mind at all and simply left where it lands
content.explanation: Waste is managed per environmental and site requirements to avoid contamination, especially in sensitive locations.
distractors: Indiscriminate drain disposal may violate rules.
Waste is not left on the ground.
Waste handling is not ignored.

content.stem: If asked to evaluate and accept welds from the data, a Level I should:
options: Refer the evaluation to a qualified higher level
Accept them all anyway just to be helpful
Reject them all anyway just to be safe
Just guess at the result and move on with it
content.explanation: Acceptance evaluation is beyond Level I qualification, so it is referred to a Level II or III rather than guessed or improvised.
distractors: Accepting beyond one's qualification is not appropriate.
Rejecting beyond one's qualification is also not appropriate.
The result is not guessed.

content.stem: Probes, wedges, and cables should be stored:
options: Protected from impact, contamination, and damage
Loose in a toolbox among all the heavy hand tools
Out in the direct sun resting on hot steel plate
Wherever happens to be the fastest on the day
content.explanation: Careful storage prevents damage that would degrade the beam or cause dead elements, keeping the equipment reliable.
distractors: Loose storage with heavy tools risks impact damage.
Heat and rough surfaces can damage probes.
Convenience does not justify risking damage.

content.stem: Acquired data and any limitations should be communicated to:
options: The responsible higher-level or supervisor
Simply no one at all on the entire job
Only the operator's own private notebook
The general public ahead of anyone else
content.explanation: Passing the data and noted limitations to the responsible person allows proper evaluation and follow-up.
distractors: Results are communicated, not withheld.
A private notebook is not the official channel.
Results go through the responsible chain, not the public.

content.stem: Because phased array setups and equipment vary, the technician should:
options: Keep skills and product knowledge current
Take all instruments as fully identical
Stop all training the moment they certify
Steer clear of all the equipment manuals
content.explanation: Equipment and software differ, so staying current with training and manuals supports correct, safe operation.
distractors: Instruments and setups are not all identical.
Competence is maintained, not stopped at certification.
Manuals are read, not avoided.

content.stem: Which statement about safety and responsibilities is correct?
options: PAUT has no radiation hazard but general safety still applies; the Level I sets up, scans, and records honestly under direction and refers evaluation to a higher level
A Level I technician goes ahead and evaluates the data and accepts or rejects the welds straight to the code on their own, with no higher level involved
The recorded data may be freely altered whenever it helps make the schedule, since hitting the deadline matters more than what the scan actually found
General site safety can be set aside entirely because phased array uses only sound, so electrical, mechanical, access, and confined-space risks need no thought at all on the job
content.explanation: Phased array has no ionizing-radiation hazard, but general industrial safety applies; the Level I acquires and records data honestly under direction and refers interpretation and acceptance to higher levels.
distractors: Evaluating and accepting welds is above the Level I.
Altering data is a serious violation.
General safety still applies despite no radiation.

content.stem: Phased-array UT of girth welds is allowed under API 1104 when the:
options: The procedure and the system are both qualified
The array carries more than sixteen elements
The operator prefers it to shooting radiography
The job has fallen behind the planned schedule
distractors: Element count alone does not qualify it.
Preference is not qualification.
Schedule is not a basis.
content.explanation: PAUT/AUT is permitted when its procedure and system are qualified per the standard.

content.stem: A Level I PAUT operator mainly:
options: Signs off the final disposition of the weld
Sets up, couples, scans, and records the data
Writes the acceptance criteria used on the scan
Qualifies the welding procedure for the joint
distractors: Disposition is above Level I.
Criteria come from the standard/company.
WPS qualification is separate.
content.explanation: Level I runs the scan and records data; evaluation and disposition sit above Level I.

content.stem: Focal laws in PAUT are used to:
options: Develop the film after the scan is complete itself
Steer and focus the beam by timing the elements
Set the radiation dose used for the joint
Cool the wedge between the scanning passes
